a)In the TED talk by Kelly McGonigal, she presented us a new perspective take on stress, which is often viewed negatively, and is harmful to our health (TED, 2013). She expressed that stress can make us healthier, by changing how we think and our mindset around the topic. She emphasizes that how we think about and respond to stress plays a crucial role in determining its impact on our well-being. 
McGonigal talks on how the neuro-hormone Oxytocin, also known as the “cuddle hormone” helps fine-tunes our brain social instincts and helps us do things that strengthen social relationships. She explains that Oxytocin also acts as a stress hormone, that is released from the pituitary glands as part of a stress response, acting like how adrenaline makes our heart pump faster. Oxytocin also acts as a natural-inflammatory by helping our blood vessels stay relaxed during stress, protecting our cardiovascular system from any effects from stress and helping the heart cells regenerate and heal from any stress-induced damage.
She further explains that Oxytocin motivates us to seek support and help, telling someone about our feelings instead of bottling it up. This creates a craving for physical contact with family and friends, also enhancing our empathy and making us more willing to help and support people who are also struggling when life gets difficult. This network of supports with human connections and caring helps strengthen our stress resilience, in turn making our stress response healthier. 
McGonigal encourages us to embrace stress instead of avoiding it. Reframing our focus on how to interpret and respond to stress, into a helpful force can help us perform better under pressure and improve our resilience.

b)Alignment with course content
McGonigal’s ideology of changing our mindsets when faced with stressful conditions is similar to what was explored in our course (Ong, 2025). Stress is commonly defined as a physiological or psychological response to internal or external stressors (APA, 2018). Aligning with the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), stress is the result of a perceived imbalance between demands and resources. The model involves two phases, starting with a primary appraisal where a person evaluates if the situation is threatening or challenging, and if it has any significant or relevant to them. In the secondary appraisal, the person then how they can deal and cope with the stressor, by evaluating the resources and coping options that are available to them to address stressful situations. This cognitive appraisal process is therefore presumed dynamic and recursive, with the quality and intensity effect of the stress response dependent on the coping strategies applied.
McGonigal also discussed that making more social and human connections can help us better manage stress, by reaching out for support instead of facing it in isolation. This illustrates the emotion-focused approach coping in the two-dimensional coping framework by Nes and Segerstrom (2006). The framework is organized into a quadrant, consisting of problem and emotion focused coping and the approach and avoidance strategies. Problem focused coping is a task-oriented form of coping, seeking out the root of the problem to solve. Emotion focused coping attempts to regulate emotions and reactions in a stressful situation. Approach coping seeks to improve the situation and reduce the negative impact of the stressors, whereas avoidance coping is passive, choosing to ignore or escape from the situation (Ong, 2025).
Critique of McGonigal’s view
There are aspects to McGonigal’s talk that require further consideration. Though she focuses on how we can reframe stress into a positive force by changing our mindset, she does not fully address the possible chronic or excessive stress can be damaging to individuals exposed long term in over-whelming or traumatic situations. A toxic workplace is an example of a prolonged exposure to stress factors, with 24% of respondents reporting such experiences. These environment drains all the energy out of them and replaced it with fear, inducing chronic stress that can lead to depression, heart disease and other illness (Sleek, 2024).
Alternative view
In comparison to stress, eustress is a positive motivating state that can enhance performance. Similarly, flow is a state of deep engagement and absorption that can also help individuals attain peak performance. The Yerkes-Dodson Law shows us a relationship between stress and task performance. The model, also known as the inverted-U model of arousal, suggests that we can reach our peak level of performance with a moderate level of stress (Pietrangelo, 2020). In the Yerkes-Dodson law, the word “arousal” refers to stress and motivation, and it only works up to a certain point, also known as the optimal level. This moderate amount of stress is manageable and motivational and can help boost your performance. Beyond this optimal level, the intense stressors perceived can lead to a fight, flight or freeze response, where one can lose focus or feel nerve-wrecking. Different individuals will have their unique optimal level, depending on several factors such as skill level, confidence and task complexity.

c)Reflecting on my encounters with stress, I would recall the period when I was re-entering the academic world as a full-time student after working for more than 20 years. I had to prepare materials for the handover at work and the administrative paperwork required for the programme of study. To ensure smooth transitions, I would be juggling the daily work operations, preparing a guide to the tasks on hand, and making time to coach the new colleague that is taking over my duties. It was both physically and mentally draining for me as my work spans across several departments and many other miscellaneous tasks. I was having a conflicting mindset of quickly handing over the tasks within a month so that I could concentrate on the new undergraduate studies, yet I was also worried if the new colleague could handle the volume of tasks I took on and if they would feel stress about it. On the other hand, I was also worried about the expectations of the new programme and whether I would be able to cope, persevere and finish the four-year study with results that I could be satisfied with.
Through the chapters of this course, I learned about the two-dimensional coping framework, that I could use the problem focused approach coping, to plan and break down the tasks on hand into more manageable ones. I could also seek additional support from colleagues and friends using the emotion focused approach coping, eliciting positive encouragement and advice from them. This is also in line with McGonigal’s talk on seeking social support instead of trying to tackle all the stressors all at once. 
With the insights from the course and TED talks, I can better understand and apply on how to manage stress more effectively and building up my resilience to prepare myself for future challenges.

How to Make Stress Your Friend by Kelly McGonigal
(https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcGyVTAoXEU)
In her TED talk, health psychologist Kelly McGonigal challenges the conventional knowledge surrounding stress and discusses the transformative impact of reframing one’s perspective on stress. The common belief that stress negatively impacts health has been taken as the gospel, with medical professionals advising people to reduce stress for better health and well-being. However, a 2011 study suggested that our thoughts on stress directly shape the body’s physical response. McGonigal explained that viewing the physical effects of stress positively transforms it into a performance-enhancing mechanism, allowing individuals to approach challenges with less anxiety and greater confidence.  She also introduced the key idea that stress-induced oxytocin production is a biological push to connect and seek support from others. McGonigal wrapped up with an empowering takeaway that life without stress has no meaning and that we should see it as a signal that we are meaningfully engaged. 
McGonigal argued that an individual's perception of stress determines its effects, and only by viewing stress in a positive light can we enhance resilience and performance. This viewpoint sharply contrasts with traditional stress research, which often emphasises the negative effects of stress on health, relationships, and productivity. 
The first idea mentioned by McGonigal, in which the perception of stress determines its effects, aligns with my learning from the Transactional Model of Stress (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), which supports this claim by distinguishing between eustress and distress, whereby stress can be beneficial to an individual if it is perceived as a challenge rather than a threat. This idea is further supported by the problem-approach method of coping. McGonigal’s views suggest that individuals develop proactive coping strategies and enhance resilience by interpreting their stress as an opportunity for growth.  
However, the effects of prolonged stress cannot be solved by changing one’s perception of it. A study found that childhood trauma could lead to disruptions in regions of the brain responsible for emotional regulation, memory processing and stress response, showing a connection between childhood trauma and lifelong brain changes (Ireton et al., 2024). Additionally, uncontrollable stressors can negatively affect mental and physical health regardless of mindset due to the helplessness associated with uncontrollable stressors. Research on students revealed that long-term academic-related stress, deemed uncontrollable due to societal expectations and external structures, “reduced academic achievement, decreased motivation and increased the risk of school dropout” (Pascoe et al., 2019). 
McGonigal also suggests that stress makes one social. She argued that oxytocin release is part of the stress response to promote social bonding and emotional support-seeking behaviours. This aligns with my learning on emotion-approach coping, where individuals actively seek social connections to manage their stress more effectively. Such forms of coping are illustrated by communities coming together in times of crisis to offer comfort and support in times of devastation and loss. 
However, when confronted with stressors, some individuals choose to engage in problem-avoidant and emotion-avoidant coping strategies, opting to withdraw, suppress emotions, or partake in maladaptive behaviours such as substance abuse. A study examining the effects of coping strategies on patients with chronic illnesses revealed a connection between avoidant coping and negative impacts on pain management and quality of life (Dindo & Lackner, 2017), while another study uncovered a correlation between avoidance coping and symptoms of poor mental health, particularly the emergence of depressive symptoms (Holahan et al., 2005). Furthermore, an overreliance on social support may lead to dependency, a quest for external validation, or evasion of tangible solutions. Such relational dynamics could culminate in unhappiness and unmet expectations, thereby increasing stress. Research from the textbook also underscores how stress can adversely affect family relationships, contradicting McGonigal’s assertion that stress universally strengthens social connections (Repetti & Wang, 2016). 
McGonigal’s last claim that the body’s stress response enhances performance is bolstered by my understanding of eustress and distress, where manageable stress levels can enhance motivation, focus and resilience. Further research indicates moderate stress levels can boost cognitive function and performance, particularly in goal-oriented tasks (Yerkes & Dodson, 1908). 
However, when faced with sustained stress, the body’s response to protect itself could prove detrimental to long-term mental and physical health. High cortisol production during times of prolonged stress is related to high dissociation scores, which are associated with the emergence and persistence of dissociative and conversion disorders (Boulet et al., 2021). Chronic stress can also lead to a host of physical health issues affecting every bodily system, such as gastrointestinal problems, immune system suppression, and cardiovascular disease (American Psychological Association, 2023). 
In conclusion, McGonigal’s TED Talk presents a compelling reframing of stress as a potential asset rather than an inherent danger. While her perspective aligns with research on eustress, coping mechanisms, and social bonding, it oversimplifies the impact of chronic stress and ignores maladaptive responses. Stress can enhance resilience in specific contexts, but its long-term effects on health and well-being cannot be dismissed, a more balanced approach would integrate both the benefits and dangers of stress, considering individual differences, environmental stressors, and coping strategies. 
Recently, as the sole senior in my dance crew, I was assigned the role of Overall-In-Charge (IC). As it was my first time being responsible for ensuring that we produced a high-quality end product, there was a significant weight on my shoulders to ensure that I was able to pull it off. However, despite my best efforts, many of my crew members, who were older than me, did not take me seriously and fooled around during practices, which resulted in lower efficiency. As such, our performance, when reviewed by our instructor, was deemed unsatisfactory, and we were forced to cancel our dance cover. Under normal circumstances, I would not have been upset by the decision as I understood that the decision would not have been easy to come to and that this decision was made for a reason. I would also not cry in front of my friends in an attempt to “weaken” the image my friends have of me. However, the stress of working towards providing the junior dancers with the experience of filming their first cover under the CCA and the perfectionist side of me being frustrated that I could not do more or do better to deal with the juniors’ disrespectful attitudes led me to break down multiple times in front of close friends, which took both them and myself by surprise. 
By taking reference to the two-dimensional coping framework in the textbook, I now understand that my response to the immense stress and disappointment was a form of emotion-focused approach. If I had known of Ms McGonigal’s TED talk and the course materials before this sequence of events, I might have been able to take the initial stress of uncooperative teammates as a challenge to work on my communication and leadership skills instead of letting the stress run its course and negatively impact me. This course and the TED talk have taught me the importance of utilising ideal stress coping to mitigate the negative impacts that result from stress, and I aim to use this as a catalyst to start applying the learnings in my daily life. By choosing to view stressors in a positive light, equipping myself with healthy coping mechanisms and actively reaching out to my social support, I am confident that I will be able to tackle any stressors in a positive light and use these challenges as a stepping stone towards becoming a more resilient person.

column2:
Charles Hunt’s TED Talk, What Trauma Taught Me About Resilience, explores how traumas cultivated his resilience. He argued that traumas can be overcome and are essential for building resilience. He shares his childhood story of growing up in 1980s California where the Black communities were affected by systemic discrimination leading to housing segregation, high unemployment rate, and other issues. Raised by a mother who was an addict, and a father involved in crimes, Charles experienced severe trauma leading to his clinical depression diagnosis in his pre-teen years. Despite facing numerous adversities, he remained hopeful and cultivated a positive attitude, allowing him to be resilient and focus on building a better future. Charles emphasises that people should see trauma as an opportunity to find their inner strength which can change their perspectives and circumstances. This will help individuals build the resilience to overcome life’s adversities.

Charles’s argument that learning to overcome trauma builds resilience aligns with Fletcher and Sarkar’s (2013) proposal that adversity and positive adaptation are the two key components of resilience. Similarly to what Charles Hunt shared, no one wants to face a negative situation. Hence, it becomes a test of how one can persevere and grow from it. The process of turning adversity into a story of growth demonstrates one’s resilience.

However, Charles Hunt’s perspective challenges the concept of the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MRR) (Richardson, 2002). MRR states that everyone starts in the state of homeostasis and adversity disrupts this comfort. Since Charles grew up in a challenging environment and faced trauma from an early stage, his life did not follow this pattern as he was born into adversities rather than experienced a disruption to his stability. This highlights the limitations of MRR as it assumes that everyone begins with stability, but many like Charles still develop resilience. Charles Hunt’s story proves that resilience may not always follow a predictable pattern hence, showing that resilience is a dynamic and not a linear process (Rutters, 2012).

Additionally, Charles’s perspective differs from the MRR classification of potential outcomes from adversities. MRR suggests that although some can successfully adapt and cultivate resilience, others are unable to cope and turn to harmful behaviour (Richardson, 2002). In contrast, Charles states that everyone can overcome life’s adversities if they adopt a positive attitude. Although Charles risks oversimplifying the complex process, choosing to persevere despite the existence of many potential responses proves one’s resilience. His journey to recovery represents MRR’s concept of resilient integration, where one builds resilience by adapting to hardships reflecting the best outcome of resilience described in MRR.

While Charles emphasises that resilience is a personal journey, research suggests that external factors can influence it. Findings from Bowes et. al.'s (2010) longitudinal study showed that warm family relationships play a significant role in building resilience. It was discovered that children who received more family warmth showed fewer behavioural issues and were more resilient to bullying. Therefore, the ability to recover from adversity does not only depend on an individual but also the existence of external support, challenging Charles’s original argument that resilience is simply a mindset and personal effort. While he overlooks the role of social support, it aligns with other important factors that Kunzler et. al. (2020) shared such as self-efficacy and optimism, which shows that personal effort is important.

Ultimately, everyone responds to adversities in vastly different ways due to an individual’s circumstances, mental strength, and other internal or external factors (Rutter, 2012). Although Charles Hunt’s personal story may challenge what MRR and other studies describes, he undoubtedly displayed strength in overcoming his trauma, showing his resilience. A commonality that the studies show, and Charles Hunt’s advice is that resilience is tested and built through facing adversities. However, resilience is shown in an individual’s ability to self-reflect, seek external support, and adopt a positive mindset to see adversity as an opportunity to grow and become resilient. 

My resilience was tested during the university application period. Since secondary school, I had a dream university that I felt would be a good place to shape my academic and personal growth. However, when I faced rejection, I felt dejected and lost. Aside from the personal disappointment of not meeting my goal, I was afraid of how society would perceive me as I did not enter the top Universities. Seeing my peers enter my dream University and sharing about their school life was a constant reminder of what I had lost. The uncertainty of my future felt overwhelming, and I struggled to stay motivated as my mental health deteriorated. 

My experience mirrored Richardson’s MRR, I began from a state of homeostasis and encountered adversity when I faced rejection. The disruption to my academic plan made my future feel uncertain. I felt stuck with thoughts of how much easier it would have been if I had been accepted. However, I realised that not moving on would not change my reality. Similarly to the potential outcomes stated in MRR, I recognised that I had the power to choose between coping and thriving from the situation or letting it consume me. 

To regain a sense of direction, I decided not to dwell on it but instead seek new goals to redefine my journey. I studied hard to attain good grades and joined interest groups where I took up leadership roles that encouraged me to step out of my comfort zone. Even on days when I doubted it could get better, I gritted my teeth and kept working hard. Likewise, in Charles’s story, even when he did not believe his situation could change, he held onto irrational hope. With a positive attitude, he graduated with a master’s degree and broke free from poverty. After my first year, my diligence paid off as I was recognised on the Academic Achievers List. This setback taught me that perseverance fuels growth which built my strength and resilience.

Kunzler et. al. (2020) listed that optimism, and positive emotions are key factors in recovering from adversity. Despite experiencing struggles, I tried to remain optimistic throughout. For instance, having a more flexible class schedule allowed me to pick up part-time jobs and explore growth opportunities. I also engaged in my hobbies and hung out with my friends, which made me happier. These happy moments gave me the strength to find my footing back and persevere through difficult times.

If I could have changed something, I would have leaned more on my peers or sought professional guidance to help process my emotions and set a clearer path. Social support is an aspect of resilience highlighted by Kunzler et al. (2020). As an overly independent person, I thought I could navigate through this challenge alone. If I had opened up sooner, I could have received the assurance and guidance to manage my emotions healthily. By allowing others to be part of my healing process, it could have made it easier to regain my footing.

Through this rejection, I learned resilience is not about avoiding failure but adapting and embracing new possibilities. I refused to let rejection define my worth and instead saw it as a turning point to reshape my journey and build a stronger mindset. This setback has led me to many opportunities that I would have otherwise not pursued. It has taught me that resilience is about actively choosing how we respond, adapt, and grow from hardships. I believe this has strengthened my resilience, and I can handle future adversities with more confidence.

column2:
The TedTalk, “How to Make Stress Your Friend” (video link) given by Kelly McGonigal explores the idea of stress being beneficial rather than harmful to us. The talk urges its listeners to widen their perspectives on stress and to reconsider the widely perceived notion that stress is detrimental to us. To support this thesis, many examples are given where it shows that those who view stress as beneficial thrive in stressful situations as compared to those who don’t. 

 The content in the talk aligns somewhat with what we have covered in the course. In the course we have touched upon the topic of eustress, in which stress is used as a motivator for overcoming tasks and can help one to grow and improve. However, I believe the talk and our course talks about stress being beneficial in different contexts. While the message of the talk is to view stress as a motivator to rise to whatever challenges we encounter, the course views stress as a motivator only when one has the resources to cope with it. While very similar, I believe they are still different. At the end of the talk, Chris Anderson, head of Ted, asks Kelly McGonigal if it would be wise for someone choosing between a stressful and non stressful job to choose the stressful job as long as they think they can handle it. She answers that it is better to chase what creates meaning in your life and to trust yourself to handle the stress that follows. Essentially, the point she is trying to convey is that just by viewing stress differently, it can radically change how you react to it, regardless of the situation you’re in, whereas the course conveys that people react well to stress when the circumstances are appropriate for it. However, not everyone agrees with this line of thinking. Many different articles and sources online disagree. One such article, titled “The myth of good stress”, believes that there is no such thing as good stress and rather what people experience when they say good stress is actually pressure. The writer believes that stress is only experienced when one is unable to cope with their situation and that this kind of stress can lead to major health problems. While the word ‘stress’ has been tossed around so much that its actual definition is up to interpretation, I believe that’s not what’s important. I believe that the points brought up in the talk hold more weight than the articles saying otherwise. Even if stress is only experienced when one is unable to cope, it does not change the situation they’re in. The only thing that can be changed is our approach and how we view stress, and I believe that is where we should be putting our focus on. However, one critique I have for this Tedtalk is the lack of real life examples. She might have given many statistics to show better performance in individuals that believe stress is beneficial, but at the end of the day that’s all they are - numbers. By providing real-life success stories it makes the message she wants to convey hold more merit and sound more believable to the audience. In spite of that, I do believe the talk was well done, and many points given are worth giving some thought.

Personally, one experience where I’ve had to deal with a large amount of stress was my final semester while I was still studying in Singapore Polytechnic. In previous semesters, I have always been very bad at handling the stress that comes during exam period - sometimes forgetting vital information during the exam or just putting in less effort in my preparation due to the fear of not meeting my expectations. However, in my last semester I had decided to change my approach towards the stress I was facing from exams. I had done precisely what was talked about in the Tedtalk. Instead of getting anxious from the stress of not performing well, I used it as a motivator - to challenge myself to rise to the occasion. This method of dealing with my stress had actually worked, and I had scored better than any of my previous semesters. Which is why I support and agree with what the talk is trying to convey. However I do have to note that while the shift in mindset had taken away the anxiety and fear I was feeling, it seems the stress was still having negative effects on me physically. When it came closer to exam week, I seemed to be having insomnia. I would struggle to fall asleep even after being awake for longer than usual periods of time and even if I did manage to fall asleep, I would always wake up in less than 7 hours and be unable to fall back asleep. One important thing to note from the course is that every individual handles stress differently. Reflecting on this incident, perhaps to fully make stress an ally, one must not only change their outlook on stress, but also develop healthy coping habits as well. In my specific context, had I consulted my friends for support or even just spent more time with family and friends, perhaps I would not have experienced insomnia. All in all, I believe the main takeaway is this -  stress can be your friend. Everyone reacts to stress differently and it is up to us to decide if it will be friend or foe. But if you don't, it will forever remain a poison that will harm your wellbeing instead of a tool that can cultivate growth.

The TED talk “The Three Secrets of Resilient People” by Lucy Hone (TEDx Talks, 2019) focused on three strategies that resilient people use to cope when facing adversities in life. The first strategy is accepting that suffering is part of every human existence which helps to prevent feelings of unfairness. The second strategy is having the ability to focus on things that can be changed, tuning in to the positives instead of being swallowed up by the negatives, thereby increasing levels of gratitude and happiness. The last strategy is asking, “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” which sets the intention to heal instead of suffering further. Hone emphasised these three strategies by first asking the audience to reflect on their own experiences of adversity as well as sharing her own personal experience, where she had to go through parental bereavement due to a car accident killing her 12-year-old daughter, Abby, together with Abby’s best friend, Ella and Ella’s mother, Sally, who was also a dear friend to Hone.
In class, I learnt that resilience refers to both the process and the results we achieve from effectively adjusting to setbacks in life. The way we think or feel can be adapted when facing adversity. I have also learnt the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (Richardson, 2003). The framework teaches us that when a disruption, such as a difficult life event, pushes us out of our comfort zone, the way we respond can result in different outcomes. It could be resilient reintegration which is the best-case scenario of growth, homeostatic reintegration which means we are brought back to our old comfort zone, reintegration with loss which means functioning at a reduced capacity or dysfunctional reintegration which is the worst-case scenario as it could be equivalent to giving up and developing maladaptive habits such as drinking. This is in line with Hone’s sharing about the car accident that pushed her out of her comfort zone and leading her to develop the three strategies, which is a case of resilient reintegration.
Additionally, we watched a video and learnt about Yip Pin Xiu (Entertainment - Mediacorp, 2023), Singapore’s six-time Paralympic gold medalist who has muscular dystrophy. Despite being disabled and treated differently by others to the extent of being bullied during her younger days in school, she had always looked at the positive side of things. Although she initially felt it was unfair and thought, “Why me? Why was I the only one with a disability?”, with her mother’s encouragement and acceptance of her disability, she eventually found a community where she belonged and discovered her calling of swimming competitively.
This aligns with Hone’s presentation on resilience, particularly on the first strategy of accepting that suffering is part of every human existence by accepting her disability, and the second strategy when she focused on the positives instead of the negatives. However, Yip Pin Xiu was able to overcome the adversity with the additional support of her mother and her community, which was a different focus from Hone’s talk. Her talk highlighted reframing of one’s mind without the help of external factors. In fact, when she first lost her daughter, she was overwhelmed by expert advice and external resources which made her feel more like a victim.
According to Luthar (2003), resilience in children is not only about inner strength or personality but is also shaped by the external environment. For example, having a protective factor, such as the child’s relationship with his or her parents, caregivers, teachers or peers. Another example is having access to social and community supports such as schools, neighbourhoods, mentoring and cultural resources. Yip Pin Xiu’s case study was able to illustrate both examples, where she had her mother and community for support, further emphasising on the external factors that affect resilience. This is also apparent in Ungar’s (2011) social ecology of resilience, where he believes that resilience is strongly influenced by one’s external environment. This means that resilience is reliant on both internal coping strategies and one’s social environment.
Personally, I had a rough upbringing from growing up in a complicated and poor family circumstance. It became apparent that it was affecting me when I did not do well for my GCE O-Levels despite being in the express stream in secondary school, making the Institute of Technical Education (ITE) the only tertiary school I could attend. While attending ITE, I managed to pull myself together and achieved my best-ever result in the first semester, a full GPA of 4.0, and eventually qualified to attend a local polytechnic. However, throughout all of that, I had always struggled with my mental health and it reached its lowest point in my third year of polytechnic. I had to seek professional and rely on my social circle. Even though financial issues persisted, causing the discontinuation of my full-time studies, I never gave up and am now working full-time while continuing studies as I had always wanted to.
I have realised throughout my journey, I struggled a lot as I often dwelled on the negativities rather than focusing on the positives. Although I have attempted to practice gratitude journaling, I did it believing that there were only positives when there are negatives, which unintentionally reinforced my negative way of thinking. For example, I only thought of writing being grateful for a friend who was there for me when someone else hurt my feelings by lying to me. Instead of feeling blessed for the friend who was there for me, I was focused on the incident, thinking “Why only me?”. This was a bad habit of mine, and something Hone described. I had to start accepting that suffering is part of every human existence and focus on the things that can be changed. If I had the acceptance and concentrated my attention on the friend who was there for me, I would not have felt that the circumstances were unfair and felt more at peace, improving my mental health.
Furthermore, it would have been extremely useful to me if I was able to utilise the third strategy by intentionally asking, “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” whenever my mental health was spiralling downwards. For example, instead of being cooped up at home with thoughts that were overwhelming me, I could have paused and evaluated if the behaviour was doing more harm than good. A step outside or connecting with my social circle could have supported my recovery. That could have helped me in my third year of polytechnic when things felt the toughest to me. By setting the intention to heal instead of suffering further, my situation could have improved much faster before my mental health reached its lowest point.
At the same time, I have learnt that my external environment was a key reason why I was able to overcome my adversity. Being able to reach out to professionals for assistance and having the support of my social circle was crucial for me. Similar to how Yip Pin Xiu managed to thrive with the encouragement of her mother and community, having these protective factors enabled me to push through the challenges in life. This reinforces that resilience does not just develop internally but also from external social environment.
With the new insights and knowledge, I will be able to better handle the next adversity in life. Firstly, knowing suffering is part of every person’s existence so I would not suffer from grievances. Secondly, focusing on what can be changed and hence, reframing my mindset into a more positive one. Thirdly, intentionally taking actions that could aid me in my healing process which could include reaching out to support systems. Lastly, learning to step out of my comfort zone and stay resilient through it all.
In conclusion, Hone’s three strategies of resilience highlights how reframing the mind to accept suffering is part of every human existence, focusing on what can be changed and intentionally asking whether our thoughts or actions help or harm us. Meanwhile, I learnt that external protective factors such as supportive relationships and community also shape resilience. All of these gave me deeper insights into my own journey on how I should have effectively dealt with the challenges I have faced and how I can better approach future adversities with resilience.

The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8NBvhAw)
In her TEDTalk, Dr. Lucy Hone shared three simple yet powerful resilience strategies that helped her got through a personal tragedy in life. She encouraged others to try these strategies to cope with adversity. Dr. Hone is a resilience expert who has supported a lot of people across several organizations and communities to recover from adversity. She has studied research and trained at University of Pennsylvania and practiced human well-being and resilience in New Zealan for a numerous of years. 
After experiencing the misfortune of losing her daughter Abi due to a car accident, Dr. Hone realized that the usual coping methods were insufficient for what she needed even though they meant well. Therefore, she conducted a self-experiment and developed three strategies that she found genuinely effective for her recovery, and she believes that it will help other people too. She supported cultivating resilient as even though it does not remove pain, it helps individuals with the ability to bounce back and continue with life. She conveyed a powerful message: “Don’t lose what you have to what you have lost” (TED, 2019).
As detailed in the video, Dr. Lucy Hone studied resilience research in Philadelphia about a decade ago and later returned to Christchurch to provide support after the earthquake misfortune. Despite her professional expertise, it was the personal tragedy of losing her own daughter, then she realized that the usual approaches such as victim support services, leaflets, and the stages of grief, made her feel overwhelmed and devastated instead of healing. This is a key point to show that everyone grieves differently. The effective way is not about following certain steps in theory, but to look within yourself and shape your thoughts and perspectives to the circumstances in a way that boosts your own mental health. 
From the beginning of her speech, the very engaging and impressive point is “Adversity doesn’t discriminate” (TED, 2019). It happens to everyone, brings us out of our homeostasis and puts us into devastation, often without warning. Hence, Dr. Lucy Hone’s first strategy is to accept that adversity can happen to anyone. The perspective shifted from self-pitying question “why me?”, to accepting the circumstance “why not me?”. It aligns with the concept of “cognitive flexibility” discussed in our course, which involves to the adaption to new challenges. By perceiving adversity as general rather than unfair personal misfortune, this strategy cultivates a self-efficacy for challenges ahead (Ong, 2023).
The second strategy is to pay attention to things that we can make impact on, correlates with the psychological principle of “optimism”. This involves analyzing the situation and focusing on things that we can change and accept those that we cannot. It supports the idea of perceiving circumstances is more important than circumstances themselves. We can’t change what has already happened, but we can choose the way we look at it and act on it. In fact, adversity reveals one’s inner strength and perspective in a positive way (Joseph, 2012).
Lastly, the third strategy is about asking yourself “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” (TED, 2019). This is a powerful tool for cultivating an agency, and the individual is an active decision maker in their recovery process. This strategy aligns strongly with the resilient factor of “active coping”, where individuals learn from setbacks and adapt their behaviors to bounce back more effectively. Through this process, individuals gradually build inner strength from their experiences rather than being fell off by them (Notebaert et al., 2025).
Even though the last strategy is undoubtedly useful, I have a different point of view on one of its aspects. Dr. Lucy Hone mentioned that while holding the daughter’s photograph and grieved, she asked herself “Is this helping or harming me?” and then put away the photo and went to bed. While I agree with the benefits of this question in terms of agency and active coping as I mentioned above, I believe the grieving process takes time. 
As per research, individuals need different timing to heal and recover from loss (Smith et al., 2025). It’s not that simple to just ask the question and move on with daily life. By not spending sufficient time to process loss, it can disrupt our daily routines. Therefore, while this strategy can bring good benefits in short term by managing behavior, in the long term, forcing oneself to shorten the grieving process can have mental health consequences.
Aligning with that is the perspective of coping with grief involves changes in the brain and learning (McCoy, 2021), which definitely takes time. The most important thing is how we can balance the sufficient time to heal, to experience pain fully with prolong grief too much. Perhaps resilience requires the ability to process pain truly first as a step before letting it go and moving on with life.
At the beginning of this year, my senior colleague resigned during the important financial year-end closing for our clients. For context, currently I am an accounts assistant at a small accounting firm near Nicoll Highway. I have started working since September 2023 and this is my first role within the accounting field. As I made a change in my career path, everything is new to me. My daily tasks were at first only data entries, and I worked under a senior who had been with the company for four years. She was supportive and taught me how to do date-entry properly. When it came to more complex accounting tasks, she told me to be patient as I needed to gain more experience and knowledge before taking on those duties.
Before her last day in February, due to time constraints, she took the initiative to complete the accounting schedules herself, thinking that she would guide me later. Unfortunately, those schedules were not done accurately, resulting in the necessity of numerous amendments by our team before they could be sent to our compilation colleagues. The worst thing was timing was not with us as my senior was about to leave the company already. After she left, I felt lost and stressed, as these clients are now under my responsibilities, and the accounts needed to be finalized by March.
To overcome these challenges, I was determined to do whatever it took to complete the work. I worked nearly every day from morning till 10 or 11pm. In the evening, when everyone left office, I was doing work while learning by using online resources and studying previous cases in company files. After going through the materials, I listed down those unresolved questions to ask my colleagues the following day, taking notes as much as I can. My focus was on the main goal of closing the accounts by the deadline, regardless of late-night sleep and how it turned my daily life upside down. My family understood the situation and encouraged me to concentrate on overcoming this period.
Eventually, after one whole month of struggles, I was able to complete the tasks even though not perfectly but acceptable. Reflecting on this experience to the course and the TEDTalk, I realized that I unknowingly applied a few resilient strategies to overcome my adversity. I did active-coping by facing the problem directly and focused on finding a solution. Furthermore, my motivation was fuel with a strong social support circle, including my family, my colleagues and boss. I’m so grateful and didn’t want to let them down.
I now understand that it would be better to perceive these circumstances as an opportunity to gain deeper accounting knowledge, rather than wondering why this situation happened to me. In addition, adopting a more optimistic mindset and better self-efficacy from the beginning might have decreased my stress levels, which was better for my mental health. Most importantly, I learned that resilience can be cultivated, it’s not a fixed trait. The course has provided me with valuable knowledge that I can apply to consistently strengthen my resilience and be able to bounce back more effectively when adversity happens.

How to Make Stress Your Friend by Kelly McGonigal
https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcGyVTAoXEU

a)In this TED talk, psychologist Kelly McGonigal takes a fresh look at stress and argues that it is not always the enemy people believe it to be. She discusses research that shows that how stress is interpreted is most important. When our body handles challenges, stress can actually benefit us. Research has shown that the racing heart and quicker breaths are signals that the body is gearing up to perform. McGonigal also talks about oxytocin, a hormone released during stressful moments that encourages people to reach out to others and strengthen their connections. This reflection will talk about how stress itself is not inherently dangerous and one’s mindset about stress can transform it into a resource for growth, resilience and deeper relationships (McGonigal, 2013).

b)The talk is closely aligned with the content covered in the course. In the course material, it was shown that stress is not always a bad thing. Sometimes, it can help as a motivator if we control it in the right way. The concept of “eustress”, or positive stress that enhances performance, closely aligns with McGonigal’s argument. Both arguments focus on how we perceive stress and cope with it, rather than simply reducing it.

However, the TED talk simplifies the complex topic. While mindset is important, research has shown chronic stress without proper coping mechanisms can have negative physiological effects such as cardiovascular disease, immune suppression and mental health disorders (American Psychological Association, 2018). McGonigal’s message may give the wrong impression that just positive thinking is enough to stop health risks. Keller et al. (2012) also show that even if perception matters, high stress for a prolonged period cannot be avoided. This shows that we need balance and a change in mindset to help us cope, which can be achieved through practicing healthy habits like time management, mindfulness and exercise.

In conclusion, McGonigal’s idea is very hopeful and gives people strength, but it is important to understand our mindset limitations. A holistic viewpoint acknowledges both the potential benefits of stress reframing and the significance of proactive stress management strategies.

c)One personal experience that connects to this talk happened during a period of intense academic pressure while preparing for a major examination. During that time, I struggled with poor sleep, headaches and constant worry about falling short. I saw stress only as something harmful and tried to escape it instead of finding constructive ways to cope with it. Procrastination became common and unhealthy habits such as stress eating developed as temporary comfort. Over time, the combination of lack of rest, physical discomfort and unhealthy coping behaviours only made the pressure feel heavier, creating a loop where stress fed into itself and became harder to manage.

Looking back through the perspectives of McGonigal’s ideas, I now recognise that the body’s reactions such as a fast heartbeat and restlessness were actually natural signals preparing me to handle the challenge. If I had interpreted those reactions as supportive rather than threatening, I could have used them to fuel motivation instead of letting them drain me. McGonigal’s point about oxytocin also highlights the value of social connections. Rather than isolating myself during my examination period, reaching out to friends or mentors for encouragement and support might have lightened the stress and built resilience.

The content covered reinforced that managing stress effectively requires both a healthy mindset and practical strategies. Approaches like structured planning, setting priorities and practicing mindfulness could have turned that stressful experience into an opportunity for growth. Taken together, McGonigal’s message together with the content covered in the course provides a balanced framework for facing future challenges with confidence, resilience and effective coping tools.

Keller, A., Litzelman, K., Wisk, L. E., Maddox, T., Cheng, E. R., Creswell, P. D., & Witt, W. P. (2012). Does the perception that stress affects health matter? The association with health and mortality. Health Psychology, 31(5), 677–684. https://doi.org/10.1037/a0026743

Stress 
How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly 
(https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc)  
  Nina in the TED talk above speaks about how to relieve stress when overwhelmed. She starts off with an example based on her own experience when she was doing her bachelor’s degree in university and was overwhelmed by all the tasks assigned. Weighing up her options, she decided to do something wholly unrelated from her studies and have fun at a party to relieve stress. She realised that she had better focus and more energy to do her work afterwards. After which she elaborated on the 3 keys to stress relief; namely – letting tension out, limiting information and lowering the barrier to entry. Letting tension out included exercise, creative and social activities and mindfulness. Limiting information helps relieve stress as according to neuroscience, the brain can only focus on 1 thing at a time. Nina speaks about a study where the brain activity of participants with short meditation breaks in between virtual meetings showed better focus compared to the other group who had consecutive meetings without any breaks. Lowering the barrier to entry refers to making activities to relieve stress more accessible and easier to carry out. Examples provided include having a dance party in your living room instead of going out for it and simply doodling and writing in bullet points when journalling instead of going out of the way to use glitter pens that makes thing more complicated. In conclusion, Nina has very succinctly and clearly described her recommended methods to relieve stress and given relevant examples to explain how they work and encourages her listeners to try them out.
  How does her TED talk tie in with Chapter 2 in the course where we discuss the topic on stress? The first example she provided regarding her college experience showed a change from distress to eustress in the secondary appraisal phase in the Transactional Model of Stress & Coping proposed by Lazarus & Folkman (1984). She did not have the energy and emotional capacity to cope with the tasks assigned and needed a break to recover from the stress. After she took a break, she felt more ready to handle the tasks. In terms of the model, she has perceived adequate resources to cope after the break. As for the 3 keys to stress relief mentioned, we can compare them with the two-dimensional framework by Nes & Segerstrom (2006) mentioned in class. All 3 keys mostly fall under emotion-focused avoidant coping where the person mentally disengages from the task to alleviate stress or emotion-focused approach coping where the person participates in social activities and receives emotional support. She emphasises the need to do something unrelated to manage stress levels as well. While this might be beneficial to the overall emotional and physical wellbeing of the person and enables the person to be more motivated to complete their tasks, she neglected to mention effective complementary problem-focused coping strategies possibly due to time constraints. According to Nes & Segerstrom (2006), different stressors might require different coping strategies to effectively tackle them. Hence problem-focused coping strategies might be better for removing stressors in situations with variables you can control. For example, after taking a break at a party to recoup her energy, she could list her numerous tasks and their due dates in order on paper and finish them one by one by priority to not feel too overwhelmed. In short, Nina could have expounded on problem-focused coping strategies as well for the benefit of her audience.
  Recently I was experiencing a very stressful period in a short stint in a customer service role. I was on the receiving end of a lot of verbal abuse and frustrations vented at me and the company. Tensions were high among colleagues due to the stressful environment. While watching the TED talk, I recognised that I was using similar coping strategies to the ones mentioned and they have proven to be effective for me. I met up with friends during the weekends at a social event with a different environment to decompress and obtain emotional support. I have also focused on enjoyable activities such as gaming and watching videos without distractions at home which are closer at hand to take my mind off things. Both have enabled me to feel more energised and less anxious about the stressors at work. I have also applied problem-focused strategies where I would write important dates and tasks down on my calendar, so I do not need to worry about forgetting them or simply packing my bag for work the night before to have an easier time in the morning before work the next day. I have also learnt new strategies to handle difficult customers during discussions with colleagues where we shared the methods by which help reduce the risk of customers becoming aggressive. These may comprise of speaking softly and staying calm so the customers will mirror the behaviour, and by making it very clear that we are trying to help them, they will have lesser reason to make things difficult for us. By practising these coping strategies and applying them in life, I am better equipped to handle the next stressful situation that appears.

Nes, L. S., & Segerstrom, S. C. (2006). Dispositional optimism and coping: A meta-analytic review. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 10(3), 235-251. https://doi.org/10.1207/s15327957pspr1003_3

Selected TED Talk: The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8NBvhAw)

“Resilient people get that shit happens” (Hone, 2019, 7:09), which is one of the few pointers which Dr. Lucy Hone outlined in her TED talk, The Three Secrets of Resilient People where she highlighted three strategies by individuals with strong mental toughness and the ability to recover from a personal trauma. 
The first pointer, as illustrated by the quote above, emphasises how people with a strong resilient capability understand and recognise that suffering and unexpected tragedies can happen to anyone (Hone, 2019). How one reacts and bounces back is key to progressing through challenges in life like personal trauma. 
The second strategy which Dr Lucy shared is focusing on acceptance of what is within one’s control for change, and what is not (Hone, 2019). As humans, the tendency to focus on the negative is a strong factor which affects the behaviour and emotions of a person in suffering. Making the effort to think positive, and focusing on things to be thankful and happy for is a factor which resilient people look to. 
Her third strategy in the form of a question which she uses as a powerful tool to ask oneself, “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me? (Hone, 2019, 12:26)” as a reflective thought, in the example of how she asks herself if revisiting old photographs or memories is helpful for the healing process, or would it be more of an emotional exhaustion by doing so (Hone, 2019). She realises the usefulness of this reflection, and a question which would benefit in other scenarios like scrolling through social media or navigating family dynamics.

The TED talk highlights about the ability for individuals to cope with the stress and focusing on the two concepts of adversity and positive adaptation which was covered as core components in seminar one on resilience. Some of the pointers which Dr Lucy talked about coincides and resonates with resilience factors includes active-coping, positive emotions and optimism. The point of view of resilience by itself should be seen as a process and the product of negative impacts from traumatic events (Rutter, 2012) and not just due to a set of traits which a person can learn or be born with. Mental health professionals have talked about the positive effects of high stress situations encourage growth for individuals (Werner, 2005), and it is important to note the balance of negative and positive emotions even for resilient personalities. Rutter (2012) encourages to relook at the idea of the response by individuals to negative emotions, and suggests stressful events can result in a better coping with stress by learning and gaining resilient traits (Rutter, 2012). Dr Lucy’s three strategies further reinforces the notion it is through tragedy and human suffering that one develops ways to cope with it, and assert control and self-confidence back in their daily lives. However, the development of resilience should be attributed to adversity and the influence of the environment of which the individual belongs to that builds up their resilience factors, which can be different from person to person. Strategies like these given by Dr Lucy would be useful to an individual if they are in the right frame of mind to employ these tips and pointers, but it may not be as relevant or valuable for someone who has not yet been in the same or faced similar stressful situation and trauma (Collins, 2008).  

One key lesson I took from this TED talk by Dr Lucy reminded me of my own struggles when my father passed away from a sickness that appeared upon his retirement after 20 years as a taxi driver. Being diagnosed with hydrocephalus overnight meant cognitive decline and incontinence - being an only child, it was a shock and swift lifestyle adjustments had to be made to care for him. Unfortunately, he was diagnosed with late stage dementia within the year, and passed on after. At that point in time, staying strong for the family as the only breadwinner and having to navigate life without my father figure and family support was tough, especially when the passing was during the period of circuit breaker due to the pandemic. I used to think resilience is a trait that is rare, and certain people have the ability to bounce back quicker than others because of the way their feelings and mindset are conditioned. This made me question the importance of growth and change in life - “How would I be able to live life again properly without a fear of losing someone close to us?” Emotionally, I struggled with facing the unknown, as I felt challenged by being out of my comfort zone and facing an environment of uncertainty – now I have a family to feed, a financial void to be filled and emotions of my mother to be managed with the passing of her husband whom she has relied on for the past four decades. 

Looking back, this experience taught me the importance and understanding of having lived and been through such stressful circumstances, we learn resilience is cultivated throughout the course of being vulnerable, taking whatever hit it is and becoming braver and stronger because of it. From what life throws at you and learning to be accepting of situations, not attaching judgement and only enough emotion to see the event through and not to break you down.
The point by Dr Lucy on asking oneself the question of “Is this helping or harming me? (Hone, 2019, 12:26)” resonated strongly with me, as that is how I learned to cope with stress and negative memories with my father’s passing as well as helping others who faced similar tragedies. It showed me the value and reinforced the idea that it is through adversity that I developed and became more open to my own feelings, being able to look for my own support system, and keeping myself in check, especially with extreme thoughts during vulnerable moments at work, with family or at the fast pace of life in Singapore. This has also changed how I view the future, learning to take things one step at a time, and most importantly, like the quote from Helen Keller, “Although the world is full of suffering, it is also full of overcoming with it. (Keller, 1903)”   
In conclusion, resilience is a process that is built on adversity and overcoming the challenges and obstacles from life which you cannot change or control. It is not a personality trait but a set of skills that one can use to develop to focus on the positives, and to navigate the dark times when one has to deal with trauma or negative emotions. The strategies presented by Dr Lucy reinforces control as a tool, reminding us it is not about avoiding the pain or grief, but to acknowledge adversity with resilience (Hone, 2019) for everyone to navigate the path towards healing and living.

Video title: What Trauma Taught Me About Resilience | Charles Hunt | TEDxCharlotte 
TED talk speaker: Charles Hunt
The message that the speaker, Charles Hunt, wanted to convey is that resilience can be built from painful memories. He shared that his adolescent days were full of negative and traumatic experiences. Having to deal with his mother, who was a drug addict, and hearing about his father, who died while incarcerated. To him, resilience meant adapting to changes and recovering from those changes as quickly as possible. He was able to bounce back and flourish in life despite suffering emotionally at a young age. He attributed it to the power of perspective and maintaining a positive attitude. He emphasised the importance of not dwelling too long on the setbacks while acknowledging reality. Having the strength to seek help from others also benefitted him greatly in overcoming his traumas. 
In essence, the speaker’s point is that we should be in conscious control of our thoughts and not let negativity take over. That and constant positive reminders to ourselves is what resilience entails.  
The course content highlighted two pivotal components of resilience: adversity and positive adaptation (Fletcher & Sakar, 2013). This is akin to the speaker’s sharing of his past experiences. He encountered family and financial adversities and overcame them through positive adaptation. The main form of adaptation was cognitive adaptation, as shown in the speaker’s emphasis on perspective shifting.
Another part which aligns in both the talk and course content is the areas that cultivate resilience (Kunzler et al., 2020). These areas include optimism, where the speaker highlighted the importance of having a positive perspective. Hardiness is also important, as the speaker mentioned the importance of being tough and prepared. The final area is social support, as the speaker believed the strength to ask for help is vital in overcoming adversities.
Overall, the talk is useful in motivating and directing people to realise that they have agency over their own lives to make things better. However, the talk was general and only covered the main goal of resilience building through traumatic experiences. It did not go into detail on the types of positive adaptation and the positive effects of resilience.
While positivity plays a crucial role in well-being, misunderstanding it could lead to toxic positivity. Toxic positivity refers to an unhealthy belief of needing to stay positive at all times, and suppressing negative emotions (Gan, 2023). How is it that something emphasised as beneficial could possibly bring about negative and potentially severe consequences?
While the speaker advocates for healthy positivity, his emphasis might lead to the misinterpretation of positivity. The issue lies within the suppression of negative emotions amidst putting up a positive front. Research shows that denying such feelings hinders healing as it makes people feel invalidated and dismissed (Putra et al., 2023). Toxic positivity stems from social relationships, often from the words of friends, family, and authority figures. As such, not only is resilience not built as a result of healing, individuals exposed to toxic positivity may even remain in silence. Several potential consequences could arise, as suppression is linked to bipolar and depressive disorders (Putra et al., 2023).
Hence, it is essential to validate one’s negative emotions on top of positive interventions to achieve psychological recovery.
One vivid experience in my life that taught me resilience was my polytechnic internship as a pharmacy student. The main adversity I faced was the morning crowd of patients. As my main role was to pick and pack medications for dispensing, watching the lists of prescriptions pile up endlessly created heavy stress. That stress slowed down my working speed and increased my frequency of mistakes, such as packing the wrong quantity. Despite my prior experience working in the food and beverage industry, I still struggled with the fast-paced environment. This generated feelings of inadequacy and self-doubt towards myself, reflecting a maladaptive response to the adversity.
According to Charles Hunt, perspective and maintaining conscious control of thoughts are key points in fostering resilience. Instead of lamenting my inability to keep up, I should have focused on my strengths instead. This could be done by consciously reassuring myself that I had done something similar before, and I can do it again. 
Apart from cognitive adaptation, positive adaptation also comes in forms such as behavioural and emotional. (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013). In this context, behavioural adaptation could be demonstrated by taking proactive actions to prepare for the crowd. By keeping the workstation tidy, the workflow would remain organised despite the long list of prescriptions waiting to be packed. Lastly, for emotional adaptation, I could be more aware of the stress felt in the present moment. This is followed by a short breathing exercise to regulate and ground my emotions. Thus, these methods of adaptation boost my confidence by allowing me to have a sense of control in what I do.
I realised that one area associated with resilience I lacked in was cognitive flexibility. My inability to appraise the situation in a more positive manner contributed to the buildup of stress and self-doubt. For instance, I could have adopted a growth mindset and focused on improvement instead of dwelling on past setbacks.
Hence, the TED talk and course content allowed me to better understand how resilience was built from that experience. I will continue to cultivate a growth mindset and be more in control of my thoughts when facing adversities.

(a) The video “The Three Secrets of Resilient People” by Dr Lucy Hone (https://youtu.be/NWH8N-BvhAw) describes Dr Hone, a resilience researcher, going through her own journey of recovery after losing her daughter, and building resilience from it. In the video, she describes three research-informed strategies that helped her:
First, accept that suffering and hardship is a part of life. When resilient people encounter difficulties, they merely think that it is normal which helps them move on. 
Second, focus on the good. This is important in our current world where we constantly face threats, and, as humans, we are wired to remember negative experiences better than the positive ones. This is also called benefit finding, which Dr Hone used to help her focus on the things she can be grateful for after her daughter’s death. 
Third, ask yourself: Is what I’m doing helping or harming me? Doing so puts the decision back into the person’s hands and helps them gain control over their life. 
(b) Dr Hone’s story and strategies to build resilience align with the theories that were covered during the seminars. She talks about how she had to cope with the loss of her daughter and how the process of it helped her become a more resilient person. That is consistent with the theory that resilience has two components: adversity and positive adaptation (Fletcher and Srakar, 2013). The loss of her daughter would be an adversity for her, and the strategies she then mentions would be the positive adaptation. This is also supported by xxx which proves that without adversity, resilience cannot be cultivated. 
The three main strategies Dr Hone mentions correspond with the strategies on cultivating resilience (Kunzler et al., 2020). The theory states that there are ten ways to build resilience: optimism, self-efficacy, active coping, cognitive flexibility, positive emotions, hardiness, social support, sense of coherence, meaning in life and religiosity. 
The first strategy: to accept that hardship is a part of life, is correlated to ‘sense of coherence’, where one is able to make sense of the situation, and manage it. This is also aligned with strategies to get out of the victim mentality, where one should take responsibility for what they can control (Cuncic, 2023). 
The second strategy Dr Hone mentions: to look for the good in the situation, correlates to the ‘cognitive flexibility’ component where one is able to use cognitive reframing (Morin, 2024) to see the positives of a situation. Benefit finding, as Dr Hone puts it, can help alleviate the negative feelings that come out of experiencing hardship, and put a person into a more positive and forward looking headspace. Here, Dr Hone also mentions that one of the positives is ‘social support’ which was essential to helping her overcome this adversity. This is supported by Harvard Business Review, which states that allowing others to support you is also a way of building relationships, and the strengthening of such relationships also contributes to resilience cultivation (Cross et al., 2021). 
The last strategy mentioned: where people ask themselves the question ‘is this helping or harming me?’ and make a decision to continue doing it or not aligns to ‘active coping’, where one is working directly on controlling something that negatively affects them and eventually builds self-efficacy (American Psychological Association, n.d.). This corroborates with the fact that unhealthy coping strategies would be avoiding the problem and, if constantly used, would be a bigger issue in the future (Morin, 2023).
(c) I encountered the most challenging period of my life in 2023. I got promoted at work, I was getting married, and facing the loss of a loved one. What looked to be positive hid many issues. The increase in workload from the promotion meant that I had to dedicate more time and energy to my job. At the same time, I had to plan a wedding which was stressful given the demands coming from both sides of the family, not to mention dealing with complicated emotions from family members. It wasn’t ideal that I could not spare much time for this, causing a strain in my relationship with my partner. On top of all that, my grandmother, who had dementia, was in the final stages of it, her mental and physical health deteriorating day by day. Emotionally and physically, I was not in a good place: I was constantly stressed and anxious, I wasn’t sleeping well or being physically active, and, perhaps due to a combination of the above, I was constantly falling sick. At times, I wanted to quit everything instead of facing up to them. 
I attribute my surviving that period of my life to the journaling habit I had for many years. Everyday, I would write down one thing I am grateful for and my feelings about the events of the day. That helped me recognise that even though there were some difficult situations I had to deal with, there were still many things in my life that I could practise gratitude for: such as my supportive parents, my partner who still loved and cared for me despite everything, and the coming together of my family to care for my grandmother. I also reminded myself that many of these things would pass: I could always quit my job if it got too much, the wedding would be done after that date, and my grandmother would be in a better place physically and mentally when she passes on. I now understand that these are aspects of resilience building. Cognitive flexibility was utilised when I did my gratitude journaling, trying to find the good in my daily life then so made me realise that not everything was bad and the world wasn’t working against me. Writing down my feelings also built my sense of coherence which helped me see that there was a limit to this difficult period, and that I was actively doing something about it. That helped me stay motivated. Through the seminars in this course, I can now see that these mental strategies were helpful in overcoming that challenging period in my life, and would continue to practise them in the future. 
From the seminars in this course and the Ted Talk, I also recognised that social support is very important in overcoming adversity and thereafter building resilience. When I was facing the aforementioned problems, I never confided in my closest family and friends, often isolating myself and feeling like I needed to deal with it alone. It stemmed from the thinking that I should not burden others with my problems. What I’ve learnt has shown me that the opposite is true and that I should seek social support in the future to better cope during difficult periods. 
Dealing with interpersonal issues isn’t my strongest suit either, I know that I can come across as brash and uncaring. So when conflict occurred due to the wedding planning, everything I said seemed to make things worse. In hindsight, I realised that I should have, as suggested by Kunzler’s research, focused on my personal values of being open-minded and accepting of others, as that would have helped me seek understanding in that moment instead of being overwhelmed by my own emotions. This would also have helped mitigate the strains caused to my relationship with my partner then. 
At work, I could have utilised more active coping and, specifically, Dr Hone’s strategy of asking myself whether this is harming or helping me. If I had done so, I would have realised sooner that the job was harming me with little benefits and I could have sought other job opportunities sooner. That would have helped me get to the root cause of my unhappiness in this aspect of my life and out of a bad work situation quicker.
