Selected TED talk: The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw)

Q1a. Summary
In her TED Talk, Lucy Hone presents three key resilience strategies from research and personal experience and demonstrates how these strategies enabled her to cope with the sudden death of her 12-year-old daughter. The first strategy involves acknowledging that hardships can happen as part of life. The second strategy pertains to the deflection of focus on what is controllable and what remains positive. The third encourages individuals to regularly ask themselves if their actions and thoughts are helping or harming them. Hone is eager to emphasise that these strategies entail an active attempt to adopt a mindset that enhances strength and healing, rather than avoidance or denial. Importantly, she reiterated that resilience is less a fixed trait than an intentional practice accessible to anyone who wants to cultivate it.

Q1b. Discussion
Lucy Hone's stance on resilience is in alignment with the core concepts taught in our course, particularly the focus on self-regulation, attitude, and the ability to cope with setbacks. Her belief that resilience involves intentional choices aligns with the growth mindset by Dweck (2006), where success can be developed through effort and adaptability and not fixed abilities. Similarly, her third strategy self-checking, aligns with self-regulation. NCO112 discusses how high achievers continuously examine and update their habits, thoughts, and behaviours to maintain performance under pressure. Hone's guidance is consistent in this sense by encouraging metacognition and personal agency to shift away from helplessness towards action. 

Her second strategy, focusing attention on what is controllable, parallels stress management covered in the course. By consciously redirecting attention to areas of agency, stress can be coped with a problem-oriented or emotions approach (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006). Her advice embodies cognitive reappraisal, a process of emotional regulation that has been shown to buffer against the effects of stress and trauma (Troy et al., 2018). For instance, instead of thinking “I failed this assignment, so I must be stupid,” a person using cognitive reappraisal might think, “This assignment was tough, but it’s a chance to learn and improve for next time.” This shift in thinking helps reduce feelings of shame or frustration and promotes a more balanced emotional response. It empowers people by reframing adversity to mitigate emotional suffering. It is the intentional, conscious exercise that sets high achievers apart from burnout performers (Heydari & Beigzadeh, 2024). 

However, while empowering, Hone's advice fails to address how structural or environmental variables shape resilience. Ungar (2018) finds that resilience is not merely an intrapersonal quality, as it's shaped by systems like environment, social support, and education. Individuals from underprivileged backgrounds or with systems-related obstacles might not find Hone's answers enough in themselves. Reinforcing this notion, the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984) suggests that intrapersonal and extrapersonal elements are in dynamic interaction—the full biopsychosocial model—when thinking about peak performance (Ong, 2025). Hence, resilience will need to be theorised contextually, with consideration of how external relationships facilitate adaptive processes. Hone's message may do a disservice to the complexity of resilience across different populations. 
Despite these limitations, her message remains valuable and simplifies key psychological concepts in an accessible way, encouraging people to develop resilience. When integrated with the more nuanced and systemic models presented in our course, her ideas become powerful tools for personal growth. Together, they remind me that resilience is not just a concept to study but a vital skill to practice. 

Q1c. Reflection
One personal experience occurred over my last year of polytechnic, when my mother was diagnosed with stage three cancer and depresssion. I remember worrying and feeling overwhelmed, especially with the long waiting times for her medical reports. At the same time, I was attempting to juggle part-time work, pressure from my final-year project, broken family dynamics and extracurricular commitments. It felt like everything was happening all at once, and I couldn’t afford to stop. Looking back, I now understand that I had no effective coping strategies and would usually self-blame, believing that I wasn't doing my best as a daughter and as a student. My thoughts became increasingly negative and self-critical, and I was constantly exhausted, both emotionally and physically. 

Hone's TED Talk helped me reframe this experience. Her first principle—"Resilient people know that suffering is part of life" was especially validating. My struggles then were something I saw as a deficiency, something that isolated me from others who were coping with it better. The assertion that trouble is a global human experience shifted my mindset. It helped me accept that it was okay to suffer, and that my reaction wasn't a failure on my part but a natural response to a challenging situation. 
The biopsychosocial emphasis of the course on optimal performance also helped me make sense of the entire scope of what I was experiencing. Emotionally, I was so stressed, but I wasn't taking care of my physical and social well-being, either—skipping meals, disrupting sleep cycles, and excluding friends. Those bad habits made things worse. 

Hone’s third principle, “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?” resonated deeply with me. Had I asked myself that question during that difficult period, I might have been more mindful to how my actions were contributing to my burnout. At that time, I perceived my emotional exhaustion as an indicator of not being resilient enough back then. Now I see that resilience is not necessarily about not being affected by adversity, but about how one recovers, learns, and adapts in relation to it. This has also helped me appreciate the value of emotional regulation strategies, like reframing my thoughts to facilitate healthier reactions to stress rather than dismissing difficult emotions. 

Reflecting on this, one of the most meaningful insights I have gained is that resilience also involves acknowledging pain, allowing space for vulnerability, and intentionally taking steps that support healing and growth. In hindsight, although I lacked the knowledge and coping mechanisms I now possess, I remain proud of how I navigated that difficult period with the emotional endurance and inner strength available to me at the time. As the common saying goes, “There are no regrets in life, just lessons.”

In the TED Talk, The Three Secrets of Resilient People, Lucy Hone shares her deeply personal and tragic story of resilience in the face of a life-altering incident. After losing her 12-year-old daughter in a car accident, Bones found that existing were victimising her, instead of giving her advice on how to control what she could. She turned to her academic background and life experiences instead, and found out that anyone can develop resilience. Three strategies allowed Bones to survive losing her child. These strategies can be applied by simply adapting them to our circumstance. Firstly, instead of asking “Why me?”, Bones accepted that hardship is part of the human experience, making it easier to move forward. Secondly, resilience is about making a conscious choice on focusing on matters you can control. Rather than being swallowed up in grief or anxiety, focusing on the good can help us stay grounded. Thirdly, constantly ask: “Is what I’m doing helping or harming me?”. Bones realised this when she kept looking at pictures of her deceased daughter realising it was harmful. This question helped her steer clear of self-destructive behaviour and thought spirals.
During this course, we spoke about going through adversity and coming out stronger as part of resilience, despite the pain. There is usually a sense of growth or continuation, like the story does not end despite adversity. Bones’ story perfectly exemplifies this, as she did not drown in grief, instead actively living and growing despite it.Bones also mentioned the positive effects of resilience, like her strategies helping her cope in her darkest hours. This aligns with class material on resilience protecting people in high-stress environments. While not mentioned in the TED Talk, resilience also improves quality of life, work happiness, and job performance, and Bones’ strategies can help achieve these goals. Bones specifically mentioned the importance of stepping out of your comfort zone. The Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency states that resilience is only built when you are pushed into unfamiliar and difficult territory (Richardson, Glenn, 2002). Bones’ story was one of extreme hardship, and her decision to confront it head-on helped her achieve resilient integration, which we discussed in class. Bones found tools, which gave her meaning, and a reason to continue growing. 
In class, we discussed personal qualities associated with resilience. Bones used optimism to intentionally focus on the good. Cognitive flexibility was utilized when she willingly adjusted her self-destructive thoughts and actions. Bones used self-efficacy when she believed she could shape her responses. She used an active coping style, rather than sitting in her grief and letting it consume her.  Despite Bones’ success story, her tragedy is one-dimensional and not applicable to everyone due to the variations in support systems, mental tools, and ability to reflect and contemplate. George Bonanno, a resilience researcher, points out that everyone reacts to trauma and hardship differently, and there is no one fixed path to resilience (Bonanno, 2021). While some may be able to use internal strategies, others require professional help, medication, or strong support systems to avoid spiraling. 
Southwick and Charney also point out how science plays a part in resilience. Biology, social networks, and community resources significantly impact how resilient we are, which was not covered by Bones. This neglects the population who face systematic issues like poverty, chronic illness, or discrimination that deter them from seeking help (Southwick, Charney, 2012). Despite this, Bones provides resilience strategies that a majority can utilize, and effectively expresses the effort needed for her to overcome tragedy, removing the mysteriousness of resilience.
While nothing compared to Bones’ story, I had my own experience with stress and failure that could have been approached differently had I known about this TED Talk. During year two in SUSS, I failed a core marketing module. While it was a difficult module, I had not expected to fail, since I had never failed anything academically before and it affected me alot. I would avoid my friends from that module, ignore homework and emails, and did not tell my parents, instead paying the reattempt fee myself, as I felt like I had let myself, and people who believed in me, down. 
After listening to class material and Bone’s talk, I realise I was engaging in self-destructive behaviours and thoughts, not helping myself get out of the loop. Bones’ strategies would have been invaluable to me at that time, allowing me to see and do things differently. I would have known to remind myself that setbacks are natural, and not the end. I would not have associated failing academically with my own self-worth, instead rationalizing it as a slip up. I could have focused on the good, like friends, family, and other classes, and that I still could retake the module. Active coping, a lesson from class, would have helped me too. I could have consulted the lecturer or studied with friends, showing self-efficacy. 
This reflection helped me realise resilience does not only apply to massive and life-altering tragedies, but also to everyday challenges. Small incidents build up over time, and with the right mindset and strategies, we avoid drowning under the pressure. By using Bones’ three strategies of accepting the situation, focusing on the good, and taking proactive steps to move forward, alongside class material of understanding the characteristics of resilience and how to apply them, I am now more prepared to face life’s challenges in healthier ways. 
In conclusion, Bones’ TED Talk reveals that resilience is not a special trait unattainable by the everyday person. We all struggle from adversity, and thus build resilience when we face them. However, to avoid unhealthy coping mechanisms, we must stick to tried and tested strategies. There is no easy way out, and effective strategies require self-awareness, effort, and choice. While Bones’ is not marketing a universal solution, her strategies are a good foundation to start on, and more importantly, they shine hope on others’ seemingly impossible situations. If she could overcome such a tragedy using her own willpower, then so can I, by altering her tools to suit my specific situation. Reflecting on my hardships, I realise that resilience is not about bouncing back from a setback, but also surging forward, using the hardship as a stepping stone to better ourselves in the future.
References:

Richardson, Glenn. (2002). The Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency. Journal of clinical psychology. Referenced from https://www.researchgate.net/publication/11523616_The_Metatheory_of_Resilience_and_Resiliency

Title: How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed by Nina Nesdoly
Speaker of the TED Talk: Nina Nesdoly
YouTube link: (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc)
(a) Short summary of TED Talk
Nina Nesdoly shares in her TED talk three ways a person could do to help them reduce stress when they are feeling overwhelmed. First, stress could be reduced by letting tension out. For instance, communicating with a close friend or having a physical workout could help to lower tension and reduce stress. Second, stress could be reduced by restricting the flow of information in. For example, taking a break away from information that causes stress such as the news could help to lower stress and improve productivity. Third, stress could be reduced by decreasing one’s barrier to entry. To specify, the activity which helps one to reduce stress does not have to be complicated. It can be as simple as journaling in point forms. The point is to take the first step in reducing stress in ways which one finds comfortable because it would help in bringing about increased energy for one to survive through their workday with higher concentration (Nesdoly, 2023). 

(b)
The TED talk content by Nina Nesdoly aligns with the course content on stress. In this case, the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984) states that stress could emerge in a person when there is an imbalance in the resources which the person has to endure with the demands. When a person is feeling overwhelmed as mentioned in the TED talk, it would suggest that the person could have undergone a primary appraisal and assessed their circumstances as threatening to them. This could result in the person to undergo in a secondary appraisal whereby the person could feel that they do not have enough resources to handle the situation. As a result, this could lead to a person feeling distress which is considered as negative result of stress. Besides, the three ways which Nina Nesdoly presents to the audience in the TED talk are coping measures to help a person achieve Eustress. To demonstrate, the TED talk suggests problem focused-approach coping strategy as suggested by Nes and Segerstrom (2006) such as engaging in a physical workout. This helps the person to cope with the stress as the stress is released through exercise. Furthermore, emotion focused-approach coping strategy such as communicating with a close friend provides emotional support to the person which helps in coping with stress (Ong, 2025).

Similarly, research has shown that nursing students have a higher tendency to adopt problem focused-approach coping strategy to handle stress. An overall improvement in well-being, learning and work performance has been reported as the advantages of utilising problem focused-approach coping strategy. In addition, the approach deals with the root cause of the problem that results in stress. In this case, the search for meaning when one is dealing with difficult circumstances and coming up with the use of different plans to tackle issues. Hence, problem focused-approach coping strategy would be regarded as the most effective method in coping with stress. However, emotion focused coping strategy handles with the feelings of the person that is associated with stress which does not deal with the root cause of the stress. For instance, nursing students were reported to have greater stress when they regularly used emotion focused coping strategy to cope with their stress. Some of the behaviours which the students had took on are watching movies, TV or sleeping to distract themselves. Furthermore, studies have also pointed that emotion focused coping strategy could result in damage to one’s health. Therefore, it could be regarded as the approach that is the least effective in coping with stress (Labrague et al., 2016). Additionally, another research considered active coping strategy to be more effective in tackling stress in contrast with avoidant coping. To illustrate, reframing negative thoughts into positive thoughts in a stressful event and making plans on how to deal with the stress are considered active coping strategies. On the other hand, avoidant coping is less effective as it causes a person to have behavioural disengagement, denial and venting (Al-Dubai et al., 2011). Thus, this suggests that it would be prudent to adopt emotion focused-approach coping as it could provide emotional support for the person from their social support system to help them in generating more positive emotions in dealing with stressors. Moreover, it would be more beneficial to avoid resorting to emotion focused-avoidance coping as attempting to create distraction through harmful behaviours such as excessive drinking would only help to cope with the problem in the short-term (Ong, 2025).

(c)
I recalled that during the period in year 2 semester 1, I felt extremely stressed out particularly when I had to prepare for my closed book exams. I have always felt that my weakness is in memorising. I struggled with trying to memorise the load of content taught for the exams and broke down several days before the exams. I remembered that before the exams, I had been working very hard to complete deadlines that come one after another and did not give myself a proper break. I also stopped engaging in my hobby which brought me joy such as gaming with friends, spending time with family and friends and exercising as I felt that there was simply not enough time. Applying the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping by Lazarus and Folkman (1984), I felt stressed because there was imbalance between the demands and resource which I had to cope. In my primary appraisal, I was worried that I would fail my exams because I could not memorise enough content and viewed it as threatening to me. In my secondary appraisal, I felt that I did not have sufficient resources to cope with the preparation of the exams and experienced distress. I had also adopted emotion focused-avoidance coping through social withdrawal. For example, I stopped spending time with my family and friends and gaming with my friends when I felt overwhelmed. As a result, this has caused me to distance myself away from my social support network and feel more stressed (Ong, 2025).

I could learn from my experience by adopting problem focused-approach coping such as having a better study plan to deal with exams in the future. Instead of cramming information in a week before the exam, I could periodically review and memorise content in the weeks leading up to the exam which could help me to retain information better. Furthermore, I could ensure that I allocate more time for studying exams such as blocking out additional days and aiming to complete my ECAs and assignments earlier. Besides, I could practise active coping by journalling down my thoughts when I feel stressed into my diary which could help me to comprehend the situation better. What’s more, I could also adopt emotion focused-approach coping by confiding with my close friends about my stressful situation. My close friends could help provide me with emotional support by encouraging me or being a listening ear. In addition, I could practise positive reinterpretation by reframing my negative thoughts into positive thoughts (Ong, 2025). The TED talk has also taught me the importance on reducing stress in a timely manner. In my experience, I had overworked myself as I kept pushing away the need to destress because I felt that I did not have enough time. Consequently, this has caused me to bottle up too much stress and become overwhelmed by it which led me to break down days before my exams. Further, I learned that reducing stress does not have to be complicated, it can be as easy as journaling down my thoughts into my diary whenever I feel stressed. Moreover, it is beneficial to take sufficient breaks as it could help me to reduce my stress and increase my productivity when I come back refreshed from my break. I could also reduce tension by going for a jog in the nature park to lower my stress.

For the purpose of this assignment, the video of choice for discussion is as follows:
?Title: The Three Secrets of Resilient People
?Speaker: Dr. Lucy Hone
?Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw


In the TED talk by Dr. Lucy Hone, an author and a researcher who did resilience research and over the years helped or supported people going through different types of adversity in their lives. Through her professional expertise and personal experience, she shared her thoughts about what it means to be resilient, how to navigate the stages of her grief and how it eventually led her to develop three key resilient strategies.

Dr. Lucy Hone said that “Adversity does not discriminate” and acknowledges that everyone goes through tough times. After losing her daughter suddenly in a car accident, she further explained how she was told that it was expected to take five years of grief, which left her feeling powerless. During that pain and anguish, she wanted to have hope, and this helped her to become actively involved in her own journey to overcome parental loss. 

Through her talk, the main message she was trying to convey to others is that it is possible to rise up from adversity, that there are workable strategies for us to adopt and it is possible to make ourselves think and act in specific ways to help us navigate through our tough times. She also shared three strategies that can be used to build our resilience.

--

In the APA Dictionary of Psychology, resilience is defined as “The process and outcome of successfully adapting to difficult or challenging life experiences, especially through mental, emotional, and behavioral flexibility and adjustment to external and internal demands” (APA,2020). There are two components to resilience – adversity and positive adaptation (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013).

In her video, the first strategy that Dr. Hone shared is that resilient people acknowledge that suffering and going through hardships are part of life. The moment this happens, one will experience a shift in mindset, which can help lift any feelings of isolation or victimization, then replaces these with hopes that one can go through tough times and instead of avoiding, they confront these challenging situations. This mindset may not be easy for everyone, but the key is acceptance, which hopefully becomes the catalyst to start making our brains work towards a more problem-solving approach. 

The second strategy was to focus on the things that we can control. It is easy to let things spiral when we are faced with adversity and when we become “frozen” from not knowing what to do or feel next. This feeling that everything is out of control, may eventually lead to an extended period of unhealthy depressive state and this will affect one’s mental, emotional and physical health. Hence, resilient people are good at identifying the good or the positive, in every emotion that surrounds them.

These first two strategies are aligned with the two components of resilience mentioned above and what was shared during the seminar lessons. Acknowledging that adversity and having to face one, is part of living and this is the first step that will help change our mindset. The videos we watched about the athlete and the parachutist showed that they did not give up and left their passion and instead gave themselves time to recuperate and do what is necessary to regain their strength and self-confidence. 

They also demonstrated how important it is to choose to look at the positive side of things instead of burying deeper into negativity. It is easier to be clouded by negative thoughts and wondering why things happen, but it is essential to be able to shift one’s energy to positivity and work towards overcoming obstacles they were facing. Having a choice is a blessing – and one should always aim to exercise our gift of choice and choose to look at the positive or to work on things are within our control.

With the right mindset and the ability to seek the positive, the third strategy that Dr. Hone shared was that resilient people can ask themselves if a thought or an action is harmful or helpful to themselves. This question is self-reflective, and one can assess whether their thoughts and actions contribute positively to their well-being. It is important to feel that we are in control of our lives again by making conscious decisions that have a positive impact on life.

I agree with Dr. Hone that these strategies do not mean that the pain will magically go away but minimally, they provide a structure to how one can start building resilience. Being constantly grateful or practicing gratitude as often as we can, will also help us to see the good in what we do, which we may have missed to see and be thankful for. 

However, I also think that having a strong support system is important and this comes even before one can start to adopt the strategies shared. With reference to the metatheory that we learnt in this module, there are four possible outcomes whenever a disruption occurs. I strongly feel that one of the most critical factors that contributes to which outcome will eventually happen, highly depends on the type of support system we have during the time of adversity. 

--

My parents divorced at one of the most critical points of my life and for a period of time, I blamed them for causing an unfortunate series of events. At the age of 15, I was unable to fathom what was happening and why it was happening. I was supposed to be preparing for a major national exam which will be pivotal in my academic journey and while I was only an occasional-A student, I knew I wanted to study hard so that I could be accepted in the school of my choice. Instead, I was faced with huge uncertainties, feelings of anger and resentment while at the same time, being forced to “grow up” as I also had a younger sibling to care for. Looking at my sibling, during those times, was what helped me focus more energy on the positive side of things instead of just being in the state of self-pity. While gratitude was the third strategy shared by Dr. Hone, I realised now that it was my first strategy during that time. I wrote down all the things that I was still grateful for despite all that happened, and I listed all the things that I could do as a 15-year-old and let the things I am unable to control to the adults. 

Things never turned out the way I planned it to be when I wrote in my book of dreams, but it made me a more resilient person who can bounce back up each time I fall.

In the TED talk video “How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed” (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9G1zyFoAaMc), Nina Nesdoly (2022) presented an evidence-based approach for stress management that includes three key strategies. The first strategy is to “Let tension out”, which is to complete the stress response cycle in our body. To do so we need to relieve the physical accumulation of stress by performing physical activities that is expressive, such as journaling, dancing, walking, talking to someone, or even crying. The next strategy is "Limit information in". Nesdoly pointed out how continuously consuming more information such as emails, news, or social media may put us in a constant stressful environment. Giving our minds the time to recuperate is important, and reducing the amount of incoming stimulation would allow our minds the space to recover. The third strategy “Lower the barrier to entry” is to engage in basic, low-effort stress-relieving activities like breathing exercises, stretching, or going outside. Nesdoly highlights the importance of consistency over intensity, stating that even minor efforts taken on a regular basis may help prevent burnout. 
After watching Nesdoly's TED presentation, I reflected on what we have learnt in class and noticed that the strategies she provided are consistent with the Two-dimensional Coping Framework (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006), which categorises stress coping strategies along two axes. The first axis, Approach versus Avoidant, distinguishes whether a coping technique is active and positive - aiming to better the circumstance, or passive and negative - attempting to flee or ignore the problem. Another axis is Problem-focused versus Emotion-focused; this determines if a coping approach is task-focused or emotion-focused - attempting to address the problem or to manage emotional responses. Approach coping is preferred over avoidant coping in this framework, regardless of whether they are problem-focused or emotion-focused. Similarly, Nesdoly calls for a shift from ignoring stress to actively managing it, highlighting the need of rest and relaxation in optimal functioning. These techniques, while accessible and neuroscience-based, may be analysed in greater depth using the Two-Dimensional Coping Framework. Some strategies shared by Nesdoly can be categorised as Emotion-focused, Approach coping. For instance, her first strategy of "let tension out", is an excellent example of Emotion-focused, Approach coping. Movement or physical release targets emotional regulation in a proactive, engaged manner. These actions allow us to respond to physiological symptoms of stress directly. According to a study, embodied coping strategies, such as deep breathing, walking, or stretching can downregulate the nervous system and promote emotional regulation (van der Kolk, 2014). Additionally, her advice to "limit information in" can be viewed as a tricky yet nuanced coping mechanism—as it may seem avoidant at a glance by disengaging with the outside world. However, it is a strategic and mindful disengagement that enables emotional rebalancing. Thus, while it may not seem to be traditionally classified as an approach strategy, it is still Emotion-focused, Approach coping as we actively plan to clear our brains to prioritise what is really important. Her last strategy, “Lower the barrier to entry” demonstrates a direct and easy way of Emotion-focused, Approach coping, encouraging small, doable acts to ease feelings of being overwhelmed. This promotes behavioural activation and continuing involvement in coping, even when comprehensive problem-solving appears impossible. By making self-care approachable, pleasant and sustainable, she enables people to build their stress coping skills, promoting progress towards more proactive stress management over time.
Nonetheless, Nesdoly’s presentation does not fundamentally address Problem-focused coping, which seeks to directly mitigate or lessen the stressors. In the Two-Dimensional Coping Framework, this dimension is crucial for building resilience, especially when the source of stress can be managed. Nesdoly’s presentation largely overlooks strategies such as task management, problem-solving, or cognitive reframing, which are strongly endorsed in the literature on adaptive coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984). For example, cognitive reframing—shifting a person's perspective on a stressor—is recognized as one of the most effective methods of Problem-focused coping, (Gross & John, 2003). This is however clearly missing from Nesdoly’s presentation. Furthermore, while Nesdoly recognises burnout as a key source of stress, her strategies focus primarily on the individual-level rather than addressing external and systemic factors to chronic stress. According to Maslach and Leiter (2016), burnout is frequently a structural issue caused by unhealthy organisational culture, poor workload management, and a lack of social support. Without taking these elements into account, Nesdoly’s presentation runs the danger of claiming that stress and burnout are purely personal management concerns, which might unfairly criticise the individual for not "coping better." Therefore, it is important that we view stress coping from a macro-level as well to prevent unhealthy misconceptions of stress management. 
Offering alternative frameworks is beneficial for presenting a more comprehensive perspective. According to the Shift-and-Persist Model (Chen & Miller, 2012), individuals from disadvantaged backgrounds often benefit from strategies that include emotional control (shift) and a sustained sense of purpose (persist), particularly in situations where stressor management is restricted. Additionally, the Salutogenic Model (Antonovsky, 1996) suggests that better health outcomes are achieved by cultivating a "sense of coherence" in which people can understand their stress and view them as controllable and purposeful. These frameworks view stress as not just one-off events but emphasise the importance of long-term resilience building through social environments and internal meaning-making. 
Personally, I have encountered intense stress during my first academic year, second semester. I was still trying to adjust myself to the school setting after five years of working full-time. I was also balancing part-time work, assignment deadlines, church services and personal responsibilities during the school term. I recall the week after the Chinese New Year holidays where I was overwhelmed by assignment deadlines. Instead of focusing on my work, I procrastinated and indulged in endless YouTube shorts as a form of coping. I was disconnected from my support system as I thought I could focus better when I was alone. Looking back, my coping response at that time involves problem avoidance, mental disengagement and self-isolation. This is Emotion-focused, Avoidant coping that did little to alleviate my stress and worsened my mental health. Now I recognize that I was trying to suppress my emotional discomfort without resolving it—an unsustainable strategy that led to exhaustion. After learning about the different stress management strategies, I can put them in practice when I am in similar situations, particularly Nesdoly’s suggestions of letting the tension out and lowering the barrier to entry. Small things such as a short walk, journaling, or even talking to friends can provide emotional relief and restore perspective. Additionally, limiting information in by reducing my social media use can reduce the noise that contributes to my stress level.
Moving forward, I aim to combine Nesdoly’s strategies, and the stress coping frameworks taught in class. By integrating both action-based and mindset-based techniques, I can approach stress in a more balanced and sustainable way. I believe effective stress management does not need huge changes, but rather a succession of incremental and deliberate decisions to care for our brains and bodies.

Nina Nesdoly, a work stress and burnout prevention consultant, speaks on stress management for individuals who feel overwhelmed. She postulates that three components are integral to relieve stress effectively. The first is to release tension from the body. She believes that the process draws something out of the individual, for example, exercising would produce sweat while journalling externalises thoughts. The second point is to limit information in. It is counterproductive to consume anxiety-inducing media content or perform multitasking during breaks. Her third point is to lower the barrier to entry. She suggests restructuring activities to reduce the resistance to engage. For example, dancing is an alternative to exercise. In essence, Nesdoly advocates that putting these three points into action would allow a stressed individual to prioritise self-care in the face of overwhelm. (132 words)

(b)
“How to Relieve Stress when You're Overwhelmed” is presented by Nina Nesdoly, a consultant for work stress and burnout prevention. She shares three components integral to stress relief, illustrating key insights through several relatable examples including research findings. Although she does not use explicit terminology, some implied messages are aligned with the course content. 
Nesdoly begins with a personal anecdote about choosing to attend a party before final exams, on top of an intense to-do list in her tertiary days. In her words, she felt completely overwhelmed by everything to be done. Her situation corresponded with the transactional model of stress and coping by Lazarus & Folkman (1984) of which interactions between her and her environment illustrated how she appraised external demands to be threatening against perceived resources to deal with them. 
Her perceived threats included term papers, final exams, and two research proposals. They were grounds for the secondary appraisal to deem that her resources were thinned out so much so that she slumped over the desk overwhelmed.
In the course content, stress is crucial for a growth mindset. So, understanding how coping strategies work could pave for optimal performance. When Nesdoly chose to party with her friend instead of working and mulling, two coping strategies were involved. One is problem-focused avoidant coping because she stopped work and disengaged from demanding tasks to give herself a break. The second is emotion-focused approach because she had enjoyed dancing with her friend, released her pent-up tension and felt happy. In the ensuing days, she felt more energised and was less stressed over her assignments.
Under conditions that seem challenging or threatening, stress can emerge as psychological and/or physiological responses (Luo et. al, 2022). After the secondary appraisal stage, one should develop adaptive coping strategies to alleviate distress as mentioned in the course. Nesdoly attributes three criteria that are based on science to make stress relief activities effective. They should let tension out of the body, limit information in, and lower the barrier to entry. 
What lets tension out
The stress relief examples that Nesdoly uses are common and yet relatable. She points out that such activities release something from the body. In the context of the biopsychosocial-spiritual model, exercise releases sweat (physiological), talking to a friend (social), journalling puts thoughts on paper (psychological), practising mindfulness through exhaling (lets go of physical tension), while a nice big hug draws out feelings of happiness and calm (psychosocial).
Why limit information in
Next, Nesdoly delves into how taking breaks might not relieve stress. The first reason is multitasking on a break. She gives an apt example of journalling while watching TV and checking emails. It has been established that the brain is wired for one task at a time. In the course notes, ‘a person’s perception or interpretation of an event as stressful is more important than the actual event itself’. Multitasking is then akin to working, by not being present enough to enjoy the experience of a true break. As such, Nesdoly suggests journal first to release the tension (putting thoughts on paper), then watch TV and check emails. 
The second reason is to abstain from social media content that creates undue fight-or-flight responses that add on to existing stressors.
Lower the barrier to entry (when)
Nesdoly has tied in this point in two directions. One is to deal with stress when already in a state of overwhelm. The other is to engage in small or simple coping activities frequently to prevent stress from building up. 
She advocates that the benefits of stress relief activities can only be felt when one would actually do it. If resistance is a factor, restructure or reframe the activities to remove the self-inflicted limitations. For example, instead of going out to party to let feelings loose, make one happen at home with the same finesse.  

(c)
This chapter on stress and coping, along with Nina Nesdoly’s TED talk presentation have given me good insights into why I am feeling very stressed nowadays, to the point that my assignment answers are cropping up in sleep since two semesters ago. With time and intentional practice, the problem and emotion-focused, approach and avoidant methods would help. 
I have enjoyed a good career in the music and media industry for almost 25 years and have never stopped learning music. Understanding how ‘eustress’ and ‘flow’ can work to  drive motivation and joy under demanding conditions have rekindled my heart’s flame to try more stuff in the future. 
This is the 9th semester with one more to go before I graduate. Academic writing has always been a handicap as I was a cameraperson, scriptwriter, and music transcriber before I retired. School went quite well in the first 7 semesters till I realise that much of what I read or learn are pushed out by new readings and research primarily for the assignments, which feels paralysing and distressing. Then Nesdoly came to the rescue and everything else is now left to my imagination. Her criteria for stress relief are sound, and the story about taking small breaks before ‘all hell breaks loose’ has been a stark wake-up call for me not to work on my assignments the way I had done with media work. I was working with competence and much love for creativity to forget the time then. As with the school assignments, I must remember I am a student eager to learn about the world, and should not allow myself to be stuck in my chair for hours on end. As how Nesdoly puts it, although I am invigorated by the love of knowledge, I realised that I must have been exhausted. This is the main reason why I am so stressed nowadays. She has also mentioned about the need to take real breaks to relieve stress. Previously, I had taken short music courses and competitions during the first six holiday breaks. I think that has left me cognitively drained for school subsequently.
Moving forward, I would use her advice and make tiny adjustments to develop proper coping strategies that would work for me, to form habits and routines that would promote active ageing.

Lucy Hone: The Three Secrets of Resilient People (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8N-BvhAw) 
(a) The speaker, Lucy shared how resilience strategies helped her cope when she lost her daughter in an accident. As a resilience expert, Lucy identified that resilient individuals have 3 common habits. Firstly, they accept that there are bad moments in life. Secondly, they intentionally choose what to focus on. Thirdly, they reflect if their actions or thoughts are harming themselves. Through her personal experience and research, Lucy emphasised that resilience is not a fixed trait and can be developed through the right mindset and behaviour. Her core message is that resilience is about making right choices to navigate through hardship.
(b Lucy’s TED talk content strongly aligns with the module’s teachings where through the Metatheory of Resilience and Resiliency (MRR; Richardson, 2002), we learned that resilience can be developed through adversity. According to MRR, all individuals start in a state of comfort that can be disrupted by stressful events, leading to 4 possible outcomes: resilient reintegration, homeostatic reintegration, reintegration with loss, and dysfunctional reintegration. The most ideal result, resilient reintegration is when the individual successfully adjusts themselves based on the disruption. Dysfunctional reintegration is the most undesirable outcome and is when the individual is unable to overcome the obstacle, thus turning to negative and dangerous actions such as substance misuse (Ong, 2025). 
In Lucy’s case, her daughter’s death was a stressful and traumatic event that disrupted her comfort zone. However, Lucy was able to develop resilient reintegration instead of remaining stuck in grieving or turning to negative coping methods. She adapted to the traumatic event and uses this experience to cultivate the 3 common habits of resilient individuals while sharing her learnings with others through public sharing. Additionally, Lucy’s experience shows the common barriers to resilient reintegration, such as individuals with negative explanatory styles tend to struggle more when overcoming obstacles as they linked the unpleasant events to internal, global, and stable factors (Ong, 2025). Lucy avoided these barriers by actively following the second habit of choosing what to focus on. Instead of focusing and dwelling on the loss of her daughter, Lucy chooses to focus on what was within her control, which was her mindset and actions. This links back to the third habit she shared on, whether your thoughts and actions are harming you. After the incident happened, Lucy found herself getting upset while looking at old photos. However, instead of blaming the driver for the incident or spiralling into negative behaviours, Lucy questioned herself if such feelings are helping or harming her. By being aware that her actions were harming her as she copes with her loss, Lucy made a conscious effort to redirect her focus by actively choosing healthier coping strategies such as caring more for her other 2 children.
However, while Lucy’s TED talk provides key insights on resilience and its importance in dealing with situations such as loss of a family member, there have been critiques on whether resilience is always desirable. Although resilience is commonly seen as a beneficial trait, there are potential disadvantages to it. Firstly, excessive resilience can lead to individuals persevering in detrimental situations without pursuing necessary changes. For example, individuals may choose to endure toxic relationships and view their endurance as resilience towards negative situations. Secondly, resilience can be mistaken for excessive optimism where individuals ignore and supress their negative emotions, leading to an inability to heal emotionally (Resilience Institute, n.d.). Excessive reliance can lead to individuals remaining stagnant in undesirable states like accepting disadvantageous situations instead of seeking positive changes (Hill et al, 2024). These differing perspectives highlights the importance of balancing resilience with self-awareness so that while developing resilience, individuals do not harm themselves.
To conclude, Lucy’s TED talk provided a real-life example of what we have learned in the module about resilience on how resilience can be developed, and it aligns closely with MRR. However, I believe that resilience should not be viewed as a trait that fits all situations. While resilience can help individuals to overcome adverse situations, it is important to maintain self-awareness and refrain from practicing resilience if it can lead to harmful outcomes. 
(c) My personal experience relating to resilience happened in the recent January 2025 school semester where I experienced the most intense burnout I have faced so far in SUSS. In my previous semesters, I would maintain a comfortable workload by taking a balanced mixture of compulsory marketing modules and SUSS core modules.  This means that I typically have only 2 to 3 open-book examinations per semester which allowed me to handle my academic workload without feeling overwhelmed by assignments and examinations. Therefore, with this balance of modules, I could still commit to my part-time work on non-school days. As shared in class, this balance is my homeostasis where it is a familiar and comfortable state, and I can function efficiently and effectively under these comfortable conditions.
This semester disrupted my homeostasis as I had completed most of my SUSS core modules and could only take on more compulsory marketing modules. This also meant that I had more examinations, including tightly packed exam dates and a closed book examination. Thus, my familiar and comfortable state of a balanced modules was disrupted. To cope with the increase in examinations, I took time off from work to focus on the examinations. However, even with an additional 3 weeks to revise, it did not feel sufficient and throughout the 3 weeks, I felt emotionally and mentally overwhelmed. Personally, I am someone who receives validation from academic achievements and uses it as a motivation during semesters. Unfortunately, this motivation became like a burden as I was slowly burning out while trying to strive for academic excellence. I was unable to remember specific details for a closed-book law module, and I did not have enough time to complete all the past year papers for most of the modules. This resulted in late night studying till 2am before a paper as a desperate attempt to remember key information. At one point, I even considered giving up on the examination as I could not remember anything no matter how hard I tried.
Looking back at this experience after this course, I now recognise that my homeostasis state was disrupted by academic overload and burnout. According to MRR, this pushes me out of my comfort zone, and I can experience any of the 4 outcomes. I initially leaned towards dysfunctional reintegration as I felt extremely exhausted and emotionally drained from the workload. However, I realised that I had reached a breaking point where I needed to make a change in my mindset. Instead of wallowing in misery over my inability to retain the necessary information or continuing to push myself without taking breaks, I applied a key habit that Lucy had shared, questioning myself if my thoughts and actions were harming me. This made me realise that by revising without breaks and staying up late to revise, I was harming my well-being and even my health as I found myself falling sick more often and having digestion problems. Therefore, with this realisation, I made a shift to focus on what I could control. I am unable to change the exam dates or the amount of time I had left for revision, but I could control my revision schedule by pacing myself better and making deliberate decisions on which modules to prioritise. By making this shift in mindset, it moved me towards a positive outcome, resilient reintegration as I was no longer trying to overcome the burnout blindly, but I was slowly trying to manage it. Through this experience, I learned that being resilient does not mean ignoring the obstacle at hand, but it is to learn how to adapt and live with it. I also learned that while academic validation is a strong motivator for me, it can easily harm me if I do not manage myself properly. Overall, this experience together with the module’s lessons and Lucy’s TED talk has taught me that resilience is not about being unaffected by the adversity, but it is about recognising what is the issue and making a positive change. 
To conclude, the learnings of this module and Lucy’s TED talk has taught me more about resilience and how it is an ongoing process. Like Lucy who used her grief to grow stronger and provide support for others, I too can use my burnout experience to better cope with heavier academic workload and expectations in the future.

TED Talk Details
Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcGyVTAoXEU
Title: How to Make Stress Your Friend
Speaker: Kelly McGonigal

Ans A) 
The message speaker, Kelly McGonigal, is trying to convey how to turn stress into a source of energy by changing the way we view, think and manage stress. 

Many people believe that stress is harmful and is linked to several health and mental issues. Kelly McGonigal's speech differs from this myth.

Firstly, she shares ways to make our body respond to it in a healthier manner instead of releasing toxic and negative energy. For example, a pounding heart shows the body is energised, while faster breathing means more oxygen for the brain. 

 Next, she shares on how to turn stress into a friend and be happier by embracing stress from a positive view. How we think and how we act can transform our experience of stress. By using case studies, she pointed out how participants in a study respond to their stress and how helpful it is to manage stress.

Lastly, how to make stress social by triggering our social instinct by enhancing our interactions with people. By using studies based on scientific outcomes, she was able to justify how we can choose to view stress as helpful and how we can connect with people under stress to build our resilience against stress. Most importantly, we are not alone in managing stress.
(McGonigal, How to make stress your friend)




Ans B)

The part where the TED talk aligns with what was covered in the seminar primarily focuses on how stress arises from an imbalance between demands and resources that are perceived by individuals and the way they choose to cope with stress. 
(S. Lazarus, PhD & Folkman, PhD, Stress arises from an imbalance between demands and resources)

Firstly, McGonigal's approach on how to change the mindset of stress syncs with the Transactional model, which show the transaction link between the person and the environment that caused stress. She explains how the person's ability to handle stress positively will be viewed as a challenge rather than a threat. The person will experience eustress rather than distress, and this support will improve the psychological and physical health of the person. 
(Stress definition and meaning | Collins english dictionary)

Secondly, McGonigal’s encourages an emotion-focused or approach-oriented view, which syncs with how to cope with stress using the Two-dimensional coping framework, where Problem vs Emotion reflects on Emotion-Focused and Approach vs Avoidant reflects on approach-oriented. (Nes & Segerstrom, 2006)

This thinking will reduce the negative impact of stress, like denial or withdrawal, and instead promote emotional support, acceptance of positive re-interpretation, and, more effectively, positive re-interpretation and well-managed stress can improve a person's performance.

Lastly, McGonigal's view that well-managed stress can enhance performance syncs with the flow of how deep engagement will result in absorption and enjoyment that is conducive for peak performance. Viewing stress as a motivator increases how a person manages challenges with skills that leads towards peak performance.

In Conclusion, McGonigal talks while using real-life examples and science to explain how to make stress your friend, which also corresponds to the seminar on the steps and how one should perceive to attain peak performance.
 
Ans C) 
Being a full-time employee and studying part-time is already a challenge where we have to juggle between family, work and studying. 
For myself, this semester was one in which I was overwhelmed with stress as I took on four modules on top of one re-sit exam. The sudden increase in study load, especially during exam period, was extremely stressful for me as compared to the two modules I used to take in previous years under another scheme.

While the initial intention was to challenge myself and take studying as a way to encourage myself to contribute better at my workplace, I overlooked the impact of how stress could take me down emotionally and mentally, especially during exam where the stress got more intense when I’m supposed to be calm, composed and focused during exam.  

I watched the TED recording and went through the seminar with Mr Carlin, I realised that while challenging myself is not wrong, the approach and method I used can be refined and better. Instead of avoiding and withdrawing by viewing stress in a negative way, I should use emotion-focused and approach-based strategies to work out a strategy when I encounter a situation and seek emotional support when needed, instead of keeping everything to myself. 

As I reflect upon myself, had I used the above method, it would have allowed the flow for me to absorb the topics more easily, have self-control and meet specific targets or goals more easily. I’m also able to think in a more positive manner. The coverage also awakened me to the fact that negative thinking will also affect my health, both mentally and physically.

Ans D) 
This reflection showcases a logical structure that uses theories and science to evaluate how different personal experiences, if applied correctly, will be able to attain the results that one desires and how to take stress in a positive manner.

How to Make Stress Your Friend by Kelly McGonigal (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcGyVTAoXEU)

In this TED talk, the speaker shares about how stress is linked to higher mortality rates but depending on the perspective of how we view stress, it can not only help us to cope with it but also push ourselves further. She argues how changing the way we think about stress can make us healthier since it changes the body's response to stress. An example would be viewing symptoms of anxiety such as faster breathing as a way of our body energising and preparing us to meet this challenge. Another point brought up was how human connection is a built-in mechanism of our stress response system for stress resilience. By caring for others or choosing to connect with those under stress, we can create stress resilience. She then ended off with an impactful quote “Go after what it is that creates meaning in your life and then trust yourself to handle the stress that follows”.
Reflecting on her talk, it opened my eyes to a whole new worldview regarding stress. External influences such as teachers, books and social media have always taught me that stress was bad which made me believe that aiming for a stress-free life is the ideal. However, she mentioned how studies have shown those who did not view stress as harmful were no more likely to die but had the lowest risk of dying as compared to everyone in the study including those who have little stress. It proves that people die not from stress but from the belief that stress is bad for you. When compared to our course materials, they both offer different takes on the impact of stress. The course materials mention how stress has negative effects on us which prevents an individual’s ability to attain peak performance. Stress can contribute to poorer academic achievement and mental health, leading to higher school dropouts for students (Ong, 2025). For adults, it can have an adverse effect on family relationships along with many other long-term consequences (Ong, 2025). However, the speaker mentions that stress is not necessarily harmful but can be beneficial if we know how to manage and utilise it well. She highlights how a change in mindset about stress can make us more social, create resilience, mitigate health problems and spur us to meet challenges head-on. 
In my opinion, both the study guide and the speaker make very valid points, however, they are both incomplete by themselves. I believe that the ideal state to achieve peak performance is a balance of both points that allows an individual to turn that stress into strength to push him or herself to achieve greater things but at the same time not overstress to the point of negatively impacting themselves. This can only be attained by understanding your stress limit and tolerance through multiple trial and error and fine-tuning the perfect amount of stress needed to achieve that state. Excessive stress is counterproductive and instead of motivating us, it will just result in chronic stress which causes symptoms from health problems to behavioural issues and that is called bad stress. (Mayo Clinic, 2023) That is when we have to use coping strategies to reduce the stress levels. On the other hand, small amounts of stress can excite us and give us the motivation to perform at our peak, that is called good stress. We can tell when we feel excited before a supposedly stressful event or having that bit of 'extra' energy to perform at our best. It keeps us on our toes to be ready for a challenge. (Healthub, 2022) Therefore, I believe that the title “Don’t Stress” in Study Unit 1, Chapter 2.1 can be rephrased to “Don’t Stress Too Much” to offer a more accurate representation instead.
While both sides offer differing views on stress, there is one point that they both align which is the coping strategies. The study guide recommends an approach-based strategy for a better long-term outcome whether it is using the problem or emotion focused-approach coping. Similarly, the speaker mentions that our body releases Oxytocin which is a stress hormone to motivate us to seek support from others and this protects our cardiovascular system as well. Furthermore, she said, “When making decisions, chasing meaning is better for your health than trying to avoid discomfort.” which I believe is a reference to approach coping strategies. Various sources online also support this argument that avoidance coping is not the way to go and procrastination approaches will just create a worsening situation. (Scott, 2024)
Regarding my personal experience, a time when I had a bit too much stress was during a semester when I doing both an internship and studying full-time taking 6 modules. It was likely overconfidence or a lack of understanding of my capabilities, I decided to take on both at the same time and thought I could manage. However, things quickly spiralled as I realised that there were too many things to do but too little time. I decided to take on everything by myself so I had to cancel meetups with friends and family and dedicate 100% of my time to either work or studying. In the end, I isolated myself from everyone and the physical and mental stress kicked in when there was no outlet and my progress for both tasks started declining rapidly. This continued until near the end of the semester when I hit my limit and fell very sick for 2 weeks before I realised my mistake. While I could still somewhat salvage my school grades, I had no choice but to request a significantly lighter workload from my internship supervisor. Fortunately, I had an understanding supervisor but I felt disappointed to have let down everyone’s expectations of me and most importantly myself, which only came to me after a costly lesson.
Reflecting upon this, it could have been better managed if I had been aware of the various coping mechanisms. What I was practicing was avoidance coping by trying to brute force my way through and pushing away help instead of the recommended approach coping which resulted in a worsening of the situation. Sometimes it is also better to listen to your body than your brain. According to the speaker, stress makes us social as Oxytocin, a stress hormone, is released to motivate us to seek support and me deciding to push away these thoughts by wanting to solve it myself just brought more harm than good. My view that stress is bad likely contributed to me falling heavily sick as it caused my body to respond negatively to this stress which affected my cardiovascular health. This experience gave me a better idea of my own stress limit and tolerance as well as my own capabilities. Lastly, I felt that the impactful quote the speaker ended with carried deep meaning and helped me better understand the experience. Despite going through this ordeal, I should not be afraid of putting myself in stressful positions again in the future. I learnt more about myself and ways to overcome it so it was a meaningful experience. Furthermore, when there are countless more opportunities in the future, there are bound to be somewhere I end up succeeding. You never know if you never try.
In conclusion, stress is a double-edged sword. It is harmful in large amounts by itself but useful if managed well. Everyone will experience it countless times in their life on the search for peak performance but only by understanding how it works will we achieve it. Ultimately, do not be afraid of stressful situations, chase after them and you will find meaning in your life.

YouTube Link: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=RcGyVTAoXEU
Title: “How to Make Stress Your Friend”
Speaker: Kelly McGonigal
(a)In her TED talk, health psychologist Kelly McGonigal challenges the typical view of stress as harmful, suggesting that stress causes harm to our health if we perceive it as such. She shared a study that argues that if an individual perceives stress as helpful, we can experience better health and improved physiological outcomes by understanding how our body reacts to stress. For example, an individual responds to an increased in heart rate as his body prepares him to face a challenging situation. She highlights the role of oxytocin, a stress hormone that helps foster social bonding and resilience. Her key message is that changing how we react to stress can support our growth and improve social connections (McGonigal, 2013).

(b)Kelly McGonigal’s TED talk aligns with the key concepts in the NCO112 course, with reference to Cultivating Resilience and Coping with Stress. Her message that mindset affects stress outcomes aligns with the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984), which states that coping with stress depends on how individuals assess a situation and how they cope with stress using the available resources. What Kelly McGonigal shared about thriving under stress is a real-world application of this model.

Her views also align with the Metatheory of Resilience (Richardson, 2002), which explains how individuals who face a difficult situation can improve in resilience and become stronger through the process. Her argument on how stress fosters social connection and helping others under stress aligns with the course materials, which highlight the importance of stress management through building resilience, supported by social support, optimism, and active coping strategies.

Kelly McGonigal’s talk did not consider a human’s complex psychological processes. For example, she based her research on a single study on the relationships between stress and health risks, where viewing stress as harmful will cause an increase in risks in one’s health. The research by Sapolsky (2004) on the analysis of chronic stress and long-term physiological damage is more convincing. The study states that long-term exposure to stress, regardless of mindset, can affect an individual’s health. 

In conclusion, Kelly McGonigal’s TED talk provides insights that complement the course content, but we should delve deeper to understand the psychological effects. Aligning her message and the course’s content will provide a balanced view of how stress can be beneficial when combined with mindset shifts, understanding our physiological state, and adopting effective coping strategies to ensure effective stress management.

(c)It was during my first year of part-time studies, and I found it challenging to cope with demands of working full-time and managing my studies and family responsibilities. It was especially tough when faced with assignment deadlines and heavy workloads. I was having difficulty adjusting and almost suffered a burnout. Somehow, I managed to overcome the stressful period. Upon reflection, I realised that I had developed ways to manage my stress by changing my view on stress. Instead of thinking negatively about it, I used it as a motivator to help me cope, which aligns with Kelly McGonigal’s (2013) argument that changing how we think about stress will help transform it into an advantage rather than a burden. I changed my mindset to view stress as a signal to prepare my body to face the challenge, which is precisely what the Transactional Model of Stress and Coping (Lazarus & Folkman, 1984) claims. Instead of being overwhelmed by work-related and academic stress, I changed my mindset. I devised a structured time-management tactic and set achievable goals, ensuring that deadlines are motivators instead of obstacles.

I remember that when I started my part-time studies, I was facing difficulty in coping as everything was new to me. I need to learn how to navigate the different SUSS systems to access the different modules and understand the requirements for each module and assignment timelines. It was a tough time for me, coupled with the heavy workload. I overcame the problem by connecting with fellow students to seek their help in understanding how to navigate the systems. This aligns with the research that seeking social support helps reduce stress and fosters resilience (Richardson, 2002). 

To overcome the tight timeline for work and assignments, I prioritized tasks and set time blocks for work that required more focus. What I did follows the Yerkes-Dodson Law, which indicates that stress helps improve performance by improving our focus and efficiency (Diamond, Campbell, Park, et al., 2007).    

To help myself to cope with stress, I decided to adopt active coping tactics. I started regular cycling, and research has shown that exercise helps reduce the physiological effects of stress (Sapolsky, 2004). Exercise helps manage our body’s cortisol levels, which in turn helps reduce stress-related fatigue. Through what I have experienced, I learned to manage stress and turn it into a motivator, which has helped to improve my ability to perform under pressure. This aligns with the Metatheory of Resilience (Richardson, 2002), which suggests that individuals experiencing a difficult situation can overcome the difficulties, resulting in positive outcomes and becoming psychologically stronger. It is a continuous journey of self-reflection and actively adopting different coping tactics to suit the situations that I may face for work, studies, or personal life. While stress remains unavoidable, we must adopt a growth mindset and have structured coping techniques to overcome future challenges. These align with what I have learned in the NCO112 course and Kelly McGonigal’s TED talk.

The Three Secrets of Resilient People by Lucy Hone (https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NWH8NBvhAw)
Summary of TED talk 
The TED talk is about a resilience researcher who gives advice based on scientific findings about resilience to help people recover from tragedy, until she was on the receiving end of a personal tragedy. When she was grieving, she realized the advice given to her by the authorities and experts was not helpful but instead hurtful. Thus, she self-experimented with her knowledge in resilience research and summarized what helped her to build resilience and overcome this difficult period of her life.
She summed up her learnings with 3 takeaways. The first takeaway is acknowledging that adversity does not discriminate and is a part of life. The second takeaway is choosing to focus on the aspects we can control instead of those we cannot, and to recognize and pivot to the positive sides of a bad situation. The last takeaway is assessing whether a particular action we are doing is helpful or harmful to us and letting go of it if it is harmful (TEDx Talks, 2019).








Alignment of TED talk content with the course coverage on resilience
The TED talk content, where Lucy Hone mentions three strategies of resilience, aligns with what we have covered in the course on resilience. The first strategy adheres to what is covered in this course on resilience, like how success does not always happen. Everyone, including successful people, faces failures and setbacks on the route to success (Ong, 2025).
The second strategy adheres to what is covered in this course on resilience, where adversity and positive adaptation are necessary for resilience (Fletcher & Sarkar, 2013). It also aligns with the areas associated with resilience under the concept of ‘bouncebackability,’ such as optimism, cognitive flexibility, and positive emotions (Kunzler et al., 2020). Resilience is built on staying positive and dealing with difficulty positively.
The last strategy aligns with ‘sense of coherence’ under the key areas of resilience building mentioned in the course (Kunzler et al., 2020). Being able to differentiate actions that help positive growth in resilience makes it easier for someone to pivot their attention towards it.
Different views on building resilience
An alternative approach to building resilience, compared to what the TED talk speaker Lucy Hone adopted for her grief recovery, includes joining social support groups. It consists of sharing sessions by others who are grieving, where participants learn how others in similar situations go through and cope with grief (Schwartz, n.d.). This is in line with how social support is important to accelerate recovery and build more resilience mentioned in the course content (Ong, 2025).
Similarly, another article mentions that resilience can be shared. We can motivate ourselves to cultivate our resilience by watching others overcome setbacks (Threads of Life, 2025). This is a fairly new viewpoint as it is not mentioned in the TED talk or the course content.
Personal experience relating to resilience 
My personal experience relating to resilience is when I was a new member of the rock climbing club in secondary school. I faced the setback of performing much worse than my teammates during our first national climbing competition, even though we joined the club at the same time. I was at the bottom of the chart against 50 other competitors and the last among my teammates in school. I was disappointed in myself when I learnt that I fared worse than my teammates. I considered giving up the sport because of my poor performance during the competition. I was plagued with self-doubt. 
However, after further thought, I started to recognize that I was just a newcomer, and one setback does not determine my success or failure in the future. There are steps I can take to improve, surpass my teammates and, most importantly, surpass myself to attain a better performance. This is in line with the course content and the first strategy of the TED talk, which helps me better understand that one has to recognize that success does not always happen. Failures and setbacks are likely to happen before achieving success.
I focused on the things that I can change and control, like keeping a positive attitude and looking forward to training sessions. I proactively sought advice from my coach on how to improve my climbing technique. I took a different perspective on the outcome of the climbing competition; at least I remained safe and injury-free, this allowed me to immediately return to training and get better after the competition. This was similar to the second strategy of the TED talk and the concept of resilience in the course content. It helps me better understand what I did was appropriate to build resilience, that I should focus on what is controllable, and look at the positive side of a difficult situation. The course content helps me learn that facing setbacks head-on instead of avoiding them, is a sign of positive adaptation to adversity, and in doing so, I am developing resilience.
There are times when I plateau with my climbing progress and get stuck at a particular climbing grade for long periods. My self-doubt builds up, and I start to think of giving up again, as it is the easy way out. However, I set myself back on track and stop thinking of trying to take the easy way out when I realize these negative thoughts are not helping me to improve. The last strategy of the TED talk made me realize I could identify what was not helpful to me. I was able to put the self-doubt aside and keep it from distracting me from improving myself.
Aside from the TED talk and course content, I was able to experience how resilience can be shared, as mentioned previously. I was motivated to press on and keep improving myself while observing my teammates overcoming their own struggles. Having a supportive social support network, which included my teammates and coach who encouraged me along the way, also helped me recover from my disappointment and self-doubt.
The course content on bouncebackability helps me better understand the areas I can adopt for future setbacks, such as self-efficacy and meaning in life, which I may not have displayed during this particular setback. I was finally able to surpass my peers and perform better at the climbing competition the following year, by clinching the top place.
 I did this by keeping my mind and body focused on what is important, which is to improve myself and be better, instead of sulking over my past performance.
